February 2, 2015
Opening
The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, February
2, 2015 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal
Center, 5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher
Reinersman presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened
with the Pledge of Allegiance. The invocation was given by Council Member
Bushong.
Proclamation – Recognizing Twenhofel Cheer Team
Mayor Reinersman presented a Proclamation to the Twenhofel Cheer Team in
recognition of their successful 2014-15 season that included taking second
runner up in the Kentucky State Cheer Competition Championship.
Roll Call
Roll was called and the following Council Members registered present: Bill
Aseere, Tom Brinker, Jim Bushong, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and Donna Yeager.
Also present was City Administrator Chris Moriconi, City Attorney John
Osterhage and City Clerk Patricia Taney.
Proclamation – Congenital Heart Defect Awareness Week
Mayor Reinersman presented to Mrs. Leslie Sams a Proclamation recognizing
February 7-14, 2015 as Congenital Heart Defect Awareness Week. Mrs. Sams stated
that four years ago her first child was born with a heart defect and that one
in 110 children is born with a congenital heart defect which is the number one
cause of infant deaths in relation to birth defects. She stated she became
involved with Little Mended Hearts which is a national organization that
provides resources and support to families. Mrs. Sams thanked Mayor Reinersman
and Council for the Proclamation and stated it’s important that we come
together as a community and raise awareness of this condition.
Request by John Karl for a Zoning Text Amendment to permit Pawn Shops in the
NSC Zone
Mayor Reinersman introduced John Karl who is interested in opening a pawn shop
in the Cherokee Plaza. Mr. Moriconi advised Council that he has been discussing
this issue with Mr. Karl who would need pawn shops added to the zoning as a
conditional use as this type of business is not currently allowed in the NSC
(Neighborhood Shopping Center) zone. He stated that as a conditional use all
pawn shops would need to go before the Board of Adjustments to get a permit.
Mr. Karl stated a conditional use is important as it would only affect the NSC
zone if the business was able to obtain the conditional use permit from the
Board of Adjustment. He stated there is no pawn shops between Walton and
Latonia. He feels that the apartment housing in the area surrounding the
Cherokee Plaza make it a perfect location for this type of business. Council
Member Brinker asked Mr. Karl if he owns pawn shops elsewhere. He stated he did
not currently own a pawn shop but has friends who do who he could rely on to
guide him in this type of business endeavor. Mayor Reinersman advised Council
this type of business is heavy regulated by the State. Council Member Yeager
stated that pawn shops were proposed for the Beechgrove Plaza in the past and
was met with resistance by this Council. Mr. Karl commented that this shop
would be located in the same building as the laundromat and the owner of the
building supports this idea. Council Member Deaton stated he spoke with the
police chief who agreed a pawn shop in this area could be a good thing and
didn’t feel it would be a crime issue. Council Member Bushong stated that his
main concern with pawn shops, when this was proposed in the Beechgrove Plaza,
was that the shop deals in the purchase/sale of guns. Mr. Karl agreed that he
would deal in the purchase/sale of guns as it is a high volume item. Council
Member Franzen commented that she recalls the proposal for a pawn shop in the
Beechgrove Plaza was denied and the owner opened as a second hand shop.
Mr. Moriconi stated the zoning text amendment process would be that the City
would make an application with PDS for the text amendment, then PDS would make
a recommendation to the City at which time the City would make a final
decision. Council Member Bushong stated he would like to review the minutes
from the past meetings when this was discussed and decided on several years
ago. Mayor Reinersman advised Council that as a conditional use this would go
before the Board of Adjustment in order to get the permit and the Board would
impose any conditions they felt necessary to allow it. Council Member Deaton
commented that the City of Covington’s ordinance regarding pawn shops is a
little beefier with a lot of detail that Independence may want to use as a
model.
Mr. Moriconi advised a Resolution to authorize the application for this text
amendment would be presented to Council at the March meeting. He stated he
would send them the meeting minutes from the past meetings where this was
discussed before the next meeting.
Request by Francie Allison for a Zoning Text Amendment to Change the Definition
of Nursery School as it Applies to School Age Children in the Residential Zone
Francie Allison, 786 Ackerly Drive, Independence – addressed Council for zoning
approval to run a State licensed Type II in-home day care facility at her
residence. She stated she currently holds a Type I license through the State
which allows her to care for up to six children in her home. She stated she
came before the City Council in 2008 for zoning approve to run the in-home day
care as her subdivision (Glenhurst), as a Planned Unit Development (PUD), did
not permit in-home day care facilities. She stated the City granted her request
in 2008 and she has since provided child care for six children in her home. She
stated that in order to provide day care for a maximum of twelve children she
will need to obtain a Type II license from the State and get zoning approval
from the City.
Council Members asked questions about her day care accommodations in her home
and if she would hire help for the additional children. She stated her husband
is retired and will help care for the children. She also advised that she has a
fenced rear yard and the lower level of her home is dedicated space for the day
care.
Mayor Reinersman asked Andy Videkovich from the Planning Commission how the
City would handle this since it is located in a PUD. Mr. Videkovich advised
that the PUD was part of the Stage I Development Plan for the Glenhurst
Subdivision and stated that no consideration was given for in-home day care
centers at the time the Plan was approved. He stated the City adopted a
Resolution amending the Stage I Development Plan in 2008 to allow in-home day
care facilities for up to six children. He stated in order to allow more than
six children the City would need to once again amend the Development Plan. He
stated the amendment would not be site specific and would apply to the entire
development. Mr. Videkovich advised there is another in-home day care center at
705 Ackerly which did not need separate approval from the City as the 2008
Resolution was for the entire development. Since this type of use was not
identified on the original Development Plan the amendment is considered minor
and can be effected by Council by Resolution.
A brief discussion ensued. Council Members inquired about the total number of
children she would care for, expressed concern about any traffic issues with
drop off and pick up of the children, health department regulations, etc. Mrs.
Allison advised that she would care for a total of twelve children which would
include any child related to her and stated that the majority of the children
she cares for live in the neighborhood so there are not any traffic problems.
She stated the health department does not inspect her facility but does provide
helpful information pertaining to health safety for child care facilities.
Council Member Yeager raised the issue about an in-home day care on Roselawn
Avenue that was not permitted. Police Captain Lucas advised that particular in-
home day care did not meet all the State qualifications and exceeded the number
of children the State would even allow.
Mr. Videkovich advised Council that allowing an in-home day care center is a
conditional use of the R-1C zone. Making it a conditional use requires an extra
step to get approval from the Board of Adjustment but that extra step would
ensure compliance in the event these in-home businesses begin to pop up
throughout the development. Mrs. Allison closed by saying she would like to
have the option of up to twelve children for short periods throughout the day,
such as before and/or after school care. Council Member Franzen stated she was
in favor of this being a conditional use which would keep it more regulated
thereby deterring less serious operators of in-home day care centers.
Mayor Reinersman stated a Resolution allowing this as a conditional use of the
Stage II Development Plan in the Glenhurst Subdivision will be drafted and on
the March agenda for Council’s final consideration.

Proposed Ordinance – Change 24 Hour Parking Limit – 1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a first reading a proposed ordinance
that would amend the City’s traffic code pertaining to parking regulations and
would increase the time a vehicle can be parked on the public ways or streets
of the City up to 72 hours or longer. He advised that current regulations
require a vehicle to be moved every 24 hours and some concerns have been
presented that suggest this time period is a short time frame especially if a
vehicle needed to be parked over the span of a weekend. He stated it has been
suggested to amend current regulations to allow for a period of up to three
days (72 hours). Mr. Osterhage read the proposed ordinance. Mr. Moriconi
commented the 24 hours period seemed to be antiquated. Mayor Reinersman assured
everyone that police officers would not be actively looking for vehicles parked
an excessive amount of time and would only respond to citizen complaints of a
vehicle that has been setting in the same spot for an unusually long period.
Ordinance No. 2014-O-04 – Providing a Credit of the Occupational License Fee
for new Employees as Part of an Economic Development Project by Balluff Inc.
under the Kentucky Business Investment Program – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2014-
O-04 that would authorize a credit of occupational license fees for a 10-year
period equal to 0.625% on the wages of new Balluff Inc. Kentucky resident
employees that would be created as part of an Economic Development Project. Mr.
Osterhage read the proposed ordinance.
A brief discussion ensued. Mayor Reinersman advised Council that he felt this
tax credit with Balluff would be good for the City as it only provides a credit
for half with the City getting the other half. Council Member Yeager expressed
some concern that Balluff would leave the City or want more at the expiration
of the ten year credit period and that this could possibly open the door for
similar requests from other businesses. Mayor Reinersman responded that it
seems to him this company is well entrenched in the City especially since they
just built an additional building on their site. He stated this credit will
only affect the new employees hired for the new building. Mayor Reinersman
advised this is additional revenue for the City, and if they do leave after ten
years, they City still comes out ahead. He stated an important upside is that
this addition to Balluff adds new jobs. Council Member Franzen agreed. Council
Member Aseere stated he advocates tax credits as incentives to new business and
that Northern Kentucky is a sandbox for commercial development.
There being no further discussion a motion was made by Council Member Aseere
and seconded by Council Member Franzen to adopt Ordinance No. 2014-O-04. Roll
was called and answered with five ayes and one no vote cast by Council Member
Bushong. Motion carried 5-1.

at all cost saving factors and mentioned that Owen Electric is also in the City

Municipal Order No. 2015-MO-01 – Appoint Tony Lucas as Police Chief
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Municipal Order No. 2015-MO-01 that would
appoint Police Captain Anthony (Tony) Lucas as Chief of Police effective August
1, 2015 upon the retirement of current Police Chief Shawn Butler. Mayor
Reinersman stated that with Shawn Butler retiring came the big decision in
finding his replacement. He thanked Council for their support during this
process and feels that he has made the right choice in selecting Tony for the
position. He stated he has complete confidence in Tony who has nearly twenty-
five years service with the City and is integrally involved in the community.
He is an outstanding member of this community having been a volunteer and Board
member of the Independence Fire District and in recent years was named Citizen
of the Year, beating out the Mayor who had also been nominated. Mayor
Reinersman went on to say that he has receive extensive law enforcement
training including the FBI National Academy which is a professional development
course for law enforcement leaders. He stated he believes the next generation
of Independence police is in good hands and trusted that Council would approve
this appointment.

Ordinance No. 2015-O-05 – Change 24 Hour On-Street Parking Limit – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-05 that would amend the City’s traffic code pertaining to parking regulations
and would increase the time a vehicle can be parked on the public ways or
streets of the City up to 72 hours or longer. Council Member Bushong asked how
the parking regulations would be enforced. Mayor Reinersman advised that police
would mark the car and then return to check the movement.
Cathy Price, 3919 Gunstock – addressed Council about the parking regulations
ordinance and stated she would like to see it enforced. She stated this is a
problem on her street and the cars will be moved when the police contact the
owner but then they move the car back after the allotted time frame and she
believes this is not the intent of the ordinance. Mayor Reinersman agreed that
people will work the system. Captain Lucas advised the revised ordinance
allowing seventy two hour will help the officers and allow residents to leave
the cars on the street for the duration of a weekend. He stated they do
community policing and will ask violators to move the cars. He stated sixty
citations have been written this year. He assured Ms. Price that the officers
are marking the vehicles and re-checking. He advised Council that Ms. Price has
be advised that she can also file a complaint at the County Clerk’s office. He
stated enforcement of this ordinance will be complaint driven. Mayor Reinersman
confirmed that the officers will not drive around the city looking to cite
vehicles that have been parked in excess of the seventy-two hours and will only
respond to complaints.
There being no further discussion, Mr. Osterhage gave Ordinance No. 2015-O-05 a
second reading. A motion was made by Council Member Yeager and seconded by
Council Member Aseere to adopt Ordinance No. 2015-O-05. Roll was called and
answered unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Discussion of Possible Zoning Text Amendment that would Allow Outdoor Dining
Areas to Provide Music and Sound Amplifying Systems as a Conditional Use in the
NSC Zones
Mayor Reinersman advised Council that the City has received the statement of
recommendation from the Kenton County Planning Commission regarding the City’s
application on a proposed text amendment to allow outdoor dining areas to
provide entertainment, music and sound amplifying systems as a conditional use
in the NSC zone. He stated they have submitted an unfavorable recommendation
which the Council can accept or the Council can override this recommendation
and move forward with the text amendment. Mayor Reinersman stated he has been
working with City Administrator Chris Moriconi on an alternative plan that
would allow outdoor music for special events and would make a zoning text
amendment unnecessary while still addressing outdoor music for special events.
He stated he feels this would resolve the issue. A citizen spoke against a
permit process for special events because he did not feel that would address
the amplified sound from televisions located in outdoor dining sections of
local restaurants like Buffalo Wild Wings or LaRosa’s. He stated those
restaurants were technically in violation of the ordinance. City Attorney
Osterhage commented that he was not sure that a television would come under the
definition of amplified sound. Mayor Reinersman explained to the citizen that
the major concern he has with allowing outdoor amplified sound in the NSC zone
is the close proximity to residential homes in the area, especially during week
nights. He feels the City will get many complaints if Council decides to move
forward with this text amendment to allow amplified sound in the NSC zone.
There being no support from Council to override the Planning Commission’s
unfavorable recommendation, Mayor Reinersman advised Council that he would
continue to resolve the outdoor amplified sound issue by working with staff in
developing a permit process that residents would need to obtain from the City
office for special events that would involve outdoor music.

The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, April 6,
2015 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal Center,
5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher Reinersman
presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened with the
Pledge of Allegiance. He then asked for a moment of silence before commencing
the meeting. Roll was called and the following Council Members registered
present: Bill Aseere, Tom Brinker, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and Donna
Yeager. Also present was City Administrator Chris Moriconi, City Attorney John
Osterhage and City Clerk Patricia Taney. Council Member Bushong was absent.
Presentation of Award to Officer Jamie Ruehl
Assistant Chief Tony Lucas introduced Lieutenant Mike Thatcher who nominated
Officer Jamie Ruehl for a department lifesaving award. Lieutenant Thatcher
stated Officer Jamie Ruehl was most deserving of this recognition for his
heroic efforts in pulling a child from a frozen pond in the Glenhurst
Subdivision in January. He stated Officer Ruehl maintained a calm exposure when
he responded to this call to find the child was below the water up to his neck.
He stated Officer Ruehl threw a rope out and instructed the child how to put
the rope around his waist all the while instructing other to call the child’s
mother and calling the life squad. He stated that he was very proud of Officer
Ruehl’ s quick thinking and composure and is very deserving of this exemplary
service. He presented Officer Ruehl with a recognition plaque.

Zoning Text Amendment Request by Ken Holliday of Huff Realty to Add Dog
Kennels, Dog Grooming and Dog Daycare facilities as a Conditional Use in the
NSC Zone
Mayor Reinersman introduced Huff Commercial realtor Ken Holliday who was
present to represent his client Allie Clegg, owner of Allie’s Walkabout, a
family owned and operated doggie day care that also provides boarding and
grooming services. Mr. Holliday advised that Allie’s Walkabout is currently a
home-based business in Villa Hills which is looking to increase and relocate to
the space formerly occupied by Kroger in the Independence Towne Center. He
stated that the Towne Center is zoned Neighborhood Shopping Center (NSC), a
zone that does not currently permit this type of use. Mr. Holliday stated the
Clegg’s are interested in the Independence area because of the City’s growth
and that statistics show that fifty percent of its residents have a dog. He
stated that Allie’s Walkabout would employ 20-30 people with round the clock
service.
Mayor Reinersman advised Council that he recently met with Mr. Holliday and the
Clegg’s and is satisfied that barking noises and odor concerns will be
addressed. Mr. Holliday stated that an aqua air central vacuum system would be
installed in the space to control odors as well as enzymatic cleaners. He
stated that all services would be contained indoors but they would offer dog
walking services to customers in their own neighborhoods. He stated they plan
on building a relationship with Pet Supply Plus which is a current tenant at
the Towne Center. In closing, Mr. Holliday requested the City approve a text
amendment application that would add dog kennels and doggie day care services
as a conditional use in the NSC zone. He stated they would even agree to the
business entrance being in the rear of the building.
A brief discussion ensued regarding signage for this type of business and
providing for entry by way of the rear of the building. Mayor Reinersman
suggested moving forward with a Resolution to approve the text amendment as the
application deadline for the Kenton County Planning Commission’s May meeting
was this Thursday Mr. Moriconi advised the Clegg’s would be responsible for the
text amendment application fee of $208. Mayor Reinersman also advised the
Clegg’s that if the final text amendment was approved by the City then the next
step would be to obtain the conditional use permit from the Kenton County Board
of Adjustment and that fee would be $550. Council Member Franzen advised the
Clegg’s that it would be a possibility that the Board of Adjustment would not
approve the permit or might put additional conditions when granting the permit.
Mayor Reinersman suggested that this type of use in the NSC zone have
additional text language that would require a rear entry to the business and
not allow signage on the main face of the building, with signage being placed
on the rear of the building. Council Member Franzen stated she was not
concerned with signage placement on the building. Council Members Yeager and

type of business.
Patrick Redden, 5301 Millcreek Circle, Independence – stated he was against a
front entrance for this type of business as he is allergic to animals. He
stated he also felt that for safety reasons the dogs should enter/exit the rear
of the building.
Mr. Holliday added that generally the landlord and tenant negotiate the
placement of the business signs. Additionally, he felt that a no “front
loading” sign would restrict front egress.
Rita Hauke, 5346 Oakview Court, Independence – stated that she felt signage on
the front of the building would be necessary for patrons to locate the
business.
Mayor Reinersman asked Andy Videkovich, Senior Planner with PDS, if the City
would be able to make changes to the text amendment recommendation from the

Presentation of Vision Plan for KY 536 Environs by University of Cincinnati
Students
Mayor Reinersman introduced Andy Videkovich, Senior Planner with PDS, who has
collaborated with University of Cincinnati Planning students to develop a plan
for KY 536. Mr. Videkovich advised Council that the Vision Plan for the KY 536
Environs study examines the potential impact of the expansion of the major
east-west corridor from Boone County to the heart of Independence. He stated
the KY 536 project has been designed and is waiting on State funding to begin
construction. He stated that OKI has begun a year-long study to determine the
impact of this road expansion on the adjacent communities. Mr. Videkovich
stated the students have explored a number of planning issues and want to hear
the City’s thoughts on the project. He stated the Plan will shed light on
possibilities for future land use along the Kenton County 536 corridor. He
stated the class’s vision and report will be used by PDA and the Planning
Commission for future land use plans along this route. Three students from U.C.
presented a power point presentation of their findings from the study which
included providing historic preservation areas and improving connectivity
through history, nature and amenities.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-06– Amending the Election Procedure to Eliminate Primary
Elections – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-06 that would forgo conducting a nonpartisan primary election for the
nomination of candidates for City office regardless of the number of candidates
running for each office. City Attorney Osterhage gave the ordinance a second
reading.
Council Member Deaton spoke in opposition to adopting this ordinance and cited
several reasons he feels primary elections should not be eliminated. Those
reasons being: low voter turnout rate, as the second fastest growing city in
Northern Kentucky a primary may be needed, anyone seriously considering
candidacy for office will be thinking of this well in advance of the general
election in November, a primary election will give a newcomer a chance to see
where they stand and the opportunity to get their name out, complaints received
from citizens in summer months are high and he was concerned there is not
enough data and information at this time to change the election process by
eliminating the primaries.
Mayor Reinersman stated this legislation was introduced after he was contacted
by the County Clerk who asked if the City would be eliminating the primary
elections now that the State has changed City classifications. He stated that
while he agrees Council Member Deaton has some valid concerns he feels that
eliminating the primary elections would broaden the field of candidates and
eliminate the confusion with two elections (primary and general) in the year.
Council Member Franzen stated that Council Member Deaton raised some good
points but admitted that candidates can get election fatigue to run two
campaigns in a year and feels the residents get tired of negative campaigns and
having candidates knocking on their door.
Patrick Redden, 5301 Millcreek Circle, Independence – commented that it is
often difficult to get people to volunteer their time as most want to sit back
and complain. He feels primary elections are needed to get serious, qualified
people.
Alan Daly, 10330 Limerick Circle – commented that if it’s not broken then it
doesn’t need to be fixed. He stated he understand that there may be a savings
to eliminate the primary election. He also feels that dedicated individuals
will look well in advance to learn of the filing deadline to file for elected
office.
Council Member Aseere voiced his support of Council Member Deaton’s concerns
and agreed that the primary election should not be eliminated.
Council Member Franzen stated she would like to table voting on this ordinance
to eliminate the primary elections until she has had more time to take this
under consideration and made a motion to do so. Motion seconded by Council
Member Aseere. Roll was called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 5-0.

The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, May 4,

Approval of the April 6, 2015 Regular Meeting Minutes
Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve the minutes of the regular

Proclamation – Building Safety Month
Mayor Reinersman read a Proclamation declaring May 2015 as Building Safety
Month supporting all government efforts to address and implement quality
building codes to protect Americans in the buildings where we live, learn,
work, worship and play.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-06 – Amending the Election Procedure to Eliminate Primary
Elections – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-06 that would forgo conducting a nonpartisan primary election for the
nomination of candidates for City office regardless of the number of candidates
running for each office. City Attorney Jack Osterhage gave the ordinance a
second reading.
Mayor Reinersman advised Council that the County Clerk contacted him earlier
this year to inquire if the City would continue holding primary elections in
light of the recent State law changing the classification of cities. He stated
that as a new “home-rule” class of city, Council can opt for or against holding
a primary election which was previously mandated when Independence was a third
class city. He stated that Erlanger and Covington are two cities that have
historically held primary elections like Independence. Mayor Reinersman stated
he supports the elimination of primary elections for a number of reasons. He
stated that in order for a primary election to occur for Council there must be
double the number of seats plus one (for a minimum of 13) to file for office.
He stated the last few elections that did not occur, so a primary election was
not held, which makes him wonder if it is worth keeping in place if it will
potentially hurt the field of candidates.
Council Member Deaton stated he didn’t feel eliminating primary elections was
right for Independence regardless of what other cities do and that everyone
should have more opportunities to exercise their right to vote each year. He
stated he was not convinced that eliminating the primary election would improve
the field of candidates and doesn’t feel the filing deadline would have an
effect on the number of candidates that would file. He stated we shouldn’t
eliminate a process that isn’t broke.
Council Member Aseere stated he agreed with Council Member Deaton’s comments
and added that if the City would decide in the future to reinstate primary
elections that it would take five years for the adjustment. Additionally, he
stated that he does not believe any savings will be realized by the City by
eliminating the primary elections.
Council Member Franzen commented that anyone that is thinking well in advance
of running for office can still file in January for the November election and
could do so anytime until the deadline in August. She stated she could vote
either way for this, but felt the primary elections historically have a low
voter turnout. She also stated that primary elections tend to be an advantage
for incumbents because if the citizens are happy with the people currently in
office then they won’t make a change. Council Member Franzen expressed concern
over the lack of candidates the last several years. She stated the democratic
process is about having a good slate of candidates on the ballot.
Council Member Brinker commented that eliminating the primary election will not
eliminate the number of candidates, just eliminate the January filing deadline.
He stated there is still the potential for an endless number of candidates.
Council Member Bushong stated he has ran seven times and feels there is no
advantage on whether or not there is a primary election. He also felt the
County Clerk’s office would realize a cost savings if the City didn’t hold a
primary election.
There being no further discussion, a motion was made by Council Member Franzen
and seconded by Council Member Bushong. Roll was called and answered with ayes
from Council Members Franzen, Bushong and Brinker and nays from Council Members
Deaton, Yeager and Aseere. Mayor Reinersman broke the tie vote by casting an
aye. Motion carried 4-3 in favor of eliminating the primary elections
(Ordinance No. 2015-O-06).
Ordinance No. 2015-O-07– Providing for a Credit of its Occupational License Fee
for New Employees for Balluff Inc. as Part of an Economic Development Project
under the Kentucky Business Investment Program – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council a proposed ordinance that would authorize
a credit of occupational license fees for wages of new Balluff Inc. Kentucky
employees that would be created as part of an Economic Development Project
under the Kentucky Business Investment Program. Mayor Reinersman reminded
Council this was originally accomplished in February of this year by way of
Ordinance No. 2015-O-04, which this proposed ordinance will amend. He stated
this new proposed ordinance has the correct tax credit of 0.5% (Ordinance No.
2015-O-04 tax credit was 0.625%). He stated that since the wrong figures were
given to the City, Balluff has agreed to pay the advertising cost of this new
ordinance. He stated the corrected rate is lower than previously stated and
adopted in Ordinance No. 2015-O-04. Mr. Osterhage gave Ordinance No. 2015-O-07
a second reading.
There being no discussion, a motion was made by Council member Franzen and
seconded by Council Member Brinker. Roll was called and answered with five ayes
and one no vote cast by Council member Bushong. Motion carried 5-1.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-08 – Amending the Schedule of Building Permit Fees – 2nd
Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-08 that would amend the schedule of fees for building permits. Mr. Osterhage
gave the proposed ordinance a second reading.
Council Member Bushong asked if these new fees were lower than the PDS and if
the City decides to contract with PDS for building inspection services, on a
permanent basis, if the City would then adopt the PDS rates. Mr. Moriconi
stated the city’s new building fee rates are still lower than those charged by
PDS. Mayor Reinersman advised that while PDS is providing temporary building
inspection services they will use the city’s new schedule of fees, but if the
city went with PDS permanently, then the PDS fees would apply. He advised
Council that he still hopes to find a replacement for Kevin Barbian (Building
Inspector) who recently resigned from the City to take another job.
There being no further discussion, a motion was made by Council Member Bushong
and seconded by Council Member Aseere to adopt Ordinance No. 2015-O-08. Roll
was called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-09 – Amending Nuisance Regulations Relating to Vacant
Buildings – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-09 amending Chapter 93.03 of the Code of Ordinances relating to nuisances to
expand the description of a nuisance as it relates to a lot, parcel or real
estate or structure. He stated this ordinance will address vacant houses that
have become a nuisance and that the City Attorney worked with the Kenton County
Attorney to draft this ordinance addressing this growing problem. Mr. Osterhage

and seconded by Council Member Brinker to adopt Ordinance No. 2015-O-09. Roll

Ordinance No. 2015-O-10 – Amending the Code of Ordinances Title IX, General
Regulations, Chapter 91, Section 91.33 and Section 91.34 Pertaining to the
Keeping and Maintaining of Animals, Vicious Dogs and Exotic and Wild Animals by
Providing Exceptions for Keeping and Controlling Same and Declaring an
Emergency – 1st Reading /and Declaration of Emergency
Mayor Reinersman advised Council that current City regulations prohibit the
keeping of wild and exotic animals. He stated the original intent of Chapter
91, Sections 33 and 34, of the Code of Ordinances was to address vicious dogs.
He stated that in order to further address this prohibition of wild and exotic
animals it would be necessary to provide for specific exceptions such as
circuses and Kenton County’s Wild Wednesdays program in Mills Park. He went on
to say that Ordinance No. 2015-O-10 is being presented for consideration to
make amendments to Chapter 91. Mayor Reinersman stated that because of the
City’s sponsorship of the Kelly Miller Circus on May 7th this ordinance is
being presented with a declaration that an emergency exists because the city
could incur financial losses if the circus cannot be held as scheduled and
there is insufficient time to schedule a special meeting for a second reading
of the ordinance. He stated the City’s legal counsel has recommended this
ordinance amendment because legal action against the City has been threatened.
He stated he would open the floor for citizen comments, but would not debate
the issue due to the threatened litigation. City Attorney Jack Osterhage read
Ordinance No. 2015-O-10.
Connie Ehlen, 10629 Williamswood Drive, Independence – addressed Council about
her opposition regarding the City’s sponsorship of the Kelly Miller Circus, the
treatment of the circus animals and she questioned the legality of changing the
City’s regulations prior to the circus event. She commented this is a
controversial issue and doesn’t feel safe to have the circus with its wild
animals in the city.
There being no further comments, a motion was made by Council Member Franzen
and seconded by Council Member Bushong to adopt Ordinance No. 2015-O-10. Roll
was called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Proposed Ordinance – Adopting an Amended 2014/2015 Budget – 1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented for a first reading a proposed ordinance that would
amend the 2014-2015 budget. There being no questions by Council, Mr. Osterhage
gave the proposed ordinance a first reading.
Proposed Ordinance – Adopting the 2015/2016 Fiscal Year Budget – 1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a first reading a proposed ordinance
that would adopt a budget for the 2015/2016 fiscal year. In his budget address
Mayor Reinersman stated he feels he addressed the needs of the City while
minimizing the impact on the citizens. He stated a particular challenge was the
declining Municipal Road Aid revenue which has resulted from the lower fuel
prices on the State gasoline tax. He stated the city’s Reserve Account will
make up the difference so that the road repairs will be the same as last year.
He stated the proposed budget will add one new police officer and maintain the
police fleet replacement schedule. He stated the Public Works Department will
also get a new truck to replace one of the older trucks. Mayor Reinersman
stated that he is optimistic for the future as he will be taking steps in
economic development and believes the City has turned the corner and is on the
verge of good things happening. He thanked the City staff for their efforts in
working with him to create a good working budget. Mr. Osterhage gave the
proposed ordinance a first reading.
Proposed Ordinance – Adopting an Employee Pay and Classification Plan – 1st

Attorney who is agreeable to amending the current agreement with the City to
include building services on a temporary basis. Mr. Osterhage read Resolution
No. 2015-R-08.
A motion was made by Council Member Aseere and seconded by Council Member
Yeager to adopt Resolution No. 2015-R-08. Roll was called and answered

Mayor’s Report – Christopher J. Reinersman

30, 2015 at Thomas More College. He stated his “Independence Team Jed” will
honor long time City Attorney Jed Deters who lost his battle with cancer in
March. He stated he is asking for pledges and hopes to raise $2,000 for the
American Cancer Society and challenged other city leaders to join him. He
stated that if he meets his goal that he, along with the City Administrator and
Assistant Police Chief Lucas will dress like a lady and do the “dude looks like
a lady” walk around the track. He stated that donations can be made at
relayforlife.com.

COUNCIL MEETING
June 1, 2015
Opening
The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, June 1,
2015 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal Center,
5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher Reinersman
presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened with the
Pledge of Allegiance and Council Member Bushong gave the invocation. Roll was
called and the following Council Members registered present: Bill Aseere, Tom
Brinker, James Bushong, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and Donna Yeager. Also
present was City Administrator Chris Moriconi and City Clerk Patricia Taney.
Executive Order 2015-O-10 – Appointment of Jack Gatlin as City Attorney
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Executive Order 2015-O-10 that would
ratify and approve a contract with attorney Jack Gatlin and Freund Freeze and
Arnold law firm to provide legal counsel to the City of Independence with Jack
Gatlin acting as City Attorney. He thanked the interim City Attorney Jack
Osterhage who graciously provided the City with legal counsel over the last
several months. Mayor Reinersman advised Council that the search for a new City
Attorney was an ardent process with a proper vetting of several law firms. He
stated that he felt the City needs a larger law firm with rock solid knowledge
of municipal law that could cover all the legal needs of a city the size of
Independence and proposed contracting with Jack Gatlin of Freund Freeze and
Arnold. Mayor Reinersman read Executive Order 2015-O-10.
A motion was made by Council member Bushong and seconded by Council Member
Aseere to approve Executive Order 2015-O-10 ratifying the appointment of Jack
Gatlin as the new City Attorney. Roll was called and answered unanimously.
Motion carried 6-0.
Mayor Reinersman welcomed Mr. Gatlin and invited him to take a seat at the
Council bench. Mr. Gatlin thanked Mayor Reinersman and the City Council for the
appointment and warm welcome.
Executive Order 2015-O-11 – Appointment of Anthony Lucas as Chief of Police
Mayor Reinersman presented Executive Order No. 2015-EO-11 appointing Anthony
Lucas as Chief of Police effective July 1, 2015. He advised that Chief Shawn
Butler will officially retire effective June 30, 2015. City Attorney Jack
Gatlin read Executive Order 2015-O-11.

Approval of the May 4, 2015 Regular Meeting Minutes

meeting held on Monday, May 4, 2015. Council Member Yeager so moved, with
second by Council Member Franzen. No amendments to the minutes were noted, roll

Pelly Road Discussion Regarding Closure and Needed Repairs
Mayor Reinersman addressed Council and the residents regarding the recent
closure of through traffic on Pelly Road between SR17 and Fowler Creek Road. He
stated that a truck hit the guardrail on the bridge near the intersection at
Fowler Creek Road and that for safety reasons the State has ordered the road
closed until the bridge can be replaced or repaired. Mayor Reinersman stated he
has been discussing all options with both State and City engineers to determine
repair or replacement of this bridge and associated costs in order to get the
road re-opened as soon as possible.
Mayor Reinersman stated this narrow, windy road cannot handle semi-trucks and
that he has heard the GPS maps are directing truckers onto this State route. He
stated the City had been addressing the signage issue to deter trucks from
using this road even before the guardrail was damaged again. And the truckers
have ignored the road signs that have been installed.
Mayor Reinersman stated that he is aware that this section of Pelly Road is a
popular route for local residents as it connects Route 16 with Route 17 and
ideally the City would want to make the necessary repairs or replace the
bridge. But this will be a major expense and the City will have to look at the
cost estimates and possible funding options. He stated one option would be to
apply for emergency State road aid. He advised the City participates in the
Municipal Road Aid Co-operative Agreement each year which allows the City to
apply for emergency funds.
At this time Mayor Reinersman opened the floor for comments from the audience.
Jim Woeste – 157 Pelly Road – suggested that Pelly Road be dead-ended and would
like Council to consider that as an option. He stated that Pelly Road is an old
country road that was never meant to handle a high volume of traffic. He stated
that he realizes making this a dead-end will inconvenience some through traffic
travelers. He stated that trucks have no business using this road and signs
will not eliminate the truckers from taking this route. He stated the Pelly
Road-Fowler Creek intersection would have to be re-designed to handle this
higher volume of traffic. He stated the new SR17 has created this additional
traffic onto their road.
Deb Egbers, 211 Pelly Road – commented that a new bridge won’t solve the
problem and suggested making Pelly Road a dead-end or building a better
connector road. She stated she has a lot of relatives that live on Pelly Road
and with the re-routing of the new SR17 and the city’s population explosion the
road is just not safe anymore. She stated the school busses have to pull over
to the side of the road to stop for pick up/drop off of the children and that
she has seen trucks back up to turn around when they find they can’t make it
through the intersection at Fowler Creek Road. She stated there needed to be a
long-term solution and not just a new bridge or repair to the bridge.
Mayor Reinersman stated he appreciated the comments and everyone is making
valid points but the City will need to also look at the cause and effects of a
permanent road closure. He agreed that Fowler Creek Road and Oliver Road were
not good alternatives for diverting traffic. Mayor Reinersman also expressed
concern for maintaining a road which only accesses twenty or so homes. He
stated the City will continue to work on a resolution to keep trucks from using
Pelly Road, perhaps installing an overpass that would keep the top of a truck
from passing through. He stated he will keep everyone posted via updates on the
City Facebook page and City website.
Gina Egbers, 221 Pelly Road – suggested installing more signage on SR17 both
north and south directions.
Mayor Reinersman advised that he would speak with the State about directional
signs that Pelly Road is closed.
Jim Woeste, 157 Pelly Road – suggested that if the City does replace/repair the
bridge and re-open the road to through traffic that speed humps be installed to
slow the traffic down.
Again, Mayor Reinersman thanked everyone for their input and advised updates
would be posted on the City Facebook page and website.
Resolution No. 2015-R-09 – Authorizing Text Amendment Application
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Resolution No. 2015-R-09 that would
authorize a zoning text amendment application that would add single family
residential dwellings in the R-2 zone. He introduced Tom Ackerman of Hearth
Home Communities who has proposed a patio home development on several acres
along Delaware Crossing between the Forest Run Subdivision and the apartment
complex. Mayor Reinersman stated the proposed development would have a lower
density than is currently zoned and that patio homes would attract empty
nesters.
Mr. Ackerman addressed Council that Hearth Homes Communities is proposing
ranch-style rental homes that will provided multiple floor plan options, of two
bedrooms, 2 baths and two car garages. He stated each unit will have high end
finishes that include granite countertops and stainless appliances. Mr.
Ackerman stated they are requesting an R-2 zone to develop ten units per acre
for a total of 78 units. He stated the original site plan, designed in the
1990’s, was for an apartment complex.
Council Member Franzen asked why they would rent instead of sell the units. Mr.
Ackerman stated it is basically a business decision to make this a rental
community as there is a strong market for this as it would not require a large
down payment or have homeowners’ association fees. He stated the monthly rental
fees would run between $1,400 - $1,700.
Mayor Reinersman commented that he did not feel the lower density would have a
negative impact on the area and that most developers would want to maximize
their site. Council Member Aseere asked about water retention. Mr. Ackerman
advised previous developers built a regional water basin in the area that will
utilized by this proposed development. Council Member Deaton asked if the
development would be constructed in phases. Mr. Ackerman advised it will be
completed at one time with site work taking three to five months and the
buildings constructed in sequential order (four months per building) so that
the development will be fully operational within 18-24 months from the start.
Council Member Bushong asked if the tenants would be charged a homeowners’ fee.
Mr. Ackerman advised there would be no homeowners’ fee but the tenants would
pay their utilities and trash service. He went on to say that Hearth Homes
would maintain all the grounds, appliances, etc.
Mayor Reinersman advised Council that the current multi-family zone would allow
more units on that site than is being proposed by Hearth Homes Communities. He
stated he feels this area would be a nice fit for the proposed patio homes. He
advised that the City’s text amendment application would be heard at the Kenton
County Planning Commission’s July 2nd public hearing and their recommendation
would be presented to Council at the August 3rd meeting.
City Attorney Gatlin read Resolution No. 2015-R-09 that would authorize the
text amendment application that would add single family residential dwellings
in the R-2 zone. A motion was made by Council Member Franzen and seconded by
Council Member Aseere to adopt Resolution No. 2015-R-09. Roll was called and
answered unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Resolution No. 2015-R-10 – Municipal Road Aid Co-Op Agreement
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Resolution No. 2015-R-10 that would
authorize the execution of the Municipal Aid Coop Program contract with the
Kentucky Transportation Cabinet for the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2015. Mr.
Gatlin read Resolution No. 2015-R-10. Mayor Reinersman explained that the coop
agreement allows the City to apply for and receive emergency funds throughout
the year from the State road aid. He stated the City has received emergency
funds in recent years for bridge and other road projects.
A motion was made by Council Member Bushong and seconded by Council Member
Franzen to adopt Resolution No. 2015-R-10. Roll was called and answered

Award Bids for Street Repairs – 2015 Street Program & Crowe Road Improvements
Mayor Reinersman introduced Public Services Director Dan Koch who would present
bid results for road repairs.
Mr. Koch advised the first project was the 2015 Street Program which includes
repairs to five streets in the Beechgrove area: Wildwood, Woodcrest, Woodknoll,
Woodmeadow and Woodtop. He stated three bids were received from JPS
Construction, Len Riegler Blacktop and Paul Michels & Sons. He stated this bid
project also included an alternate bid for the complete repair of Timber Lane
which runs off of Bristow Road. Mr. Koch recommended awarding the bid for both
the base bid for the streets in Beechgrove ($400,375) and the alternate bid of
Timber Lane ($227,088.75). He also recommended awarding the bid to JPS
Construction as the best and lowest bid for the total bid amount of
$627,463.75. Mayor Reinersman agreed that it would be best to repair all these
streets at one time since the contractor will be in the same general area.
A motion was made by Council Member Yeager and seconded by Council Member
Aseere to award the 2015 Street Repair Program bids including the alternate bid
for repairs to Timber Lane to JPS Construction in the amount of $627,463.75.
Roll was called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Mr. Koch presented the bid proposals for the Crowe Road Improvements. He stated
two bids were received: Paul Michels & Sons in the amount of $47,402.50 and Len
Riegler Blacktop in the amount of $68,175.00. He stated the low bid came in
lower than the city engineer’s estimated cost. Mr. Koch advised that the City
has applied for emergency road aid to realign this road and repair the
embankment as the road is slipping into the creek. Council Member Bushong
questioned if this was previously realigned. Mr. Koch stated that Crowe Road
had a bridge replacement several years ago, not a realignment. Council Member
Franzen asked if the realignment would be a temporary or permanent fix. Mr.
Koch advised the road has been piered in two areas and this realignment would
be a permanent fix and should not need additional work for a long time.
There being no further discussion, a motion was made by Council Member Aseere
and seconded by Council Member Franzen to award the Crowe Road Improvements bid
to Paul Michels & Sons in the amount of $47,402.50. Roll was called and
answered unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.

Resolution No. 2015-R-12 Approving a Stage II Development Plan in the
Courthouse Crossing and Located in a GMU Zone
Mayor Reinersman presented Resolution No. 2015-R-12, which would approve a
Stage II Development Plan in the Courthouse Crossing development which is
located in a GMU zone. He stated Council would need to discuss any conditions
they would require for approval and insert the conditional language in this
Resolution. Mayor Reinersman introduced Bob Schroeder of Arlinghaus Builders
who sold the parcel to Jessica Ballard who proposes to construct a daycare
facility (Kentucky Learning Center) on the 1.9 acre site. The Courthouse
Crossing development is located at the corner of McCullum Pike and the New
SR17.
Mr. Schroeder advised the Kenton County Planning Commission has recommended
disapproval of this proposed Stage II plan for several reasons, but he feels
the proposed building, next to the St. Elizabeth medical building, will be a
perfect mix for the zone. He stated Ms. Ballard would like to stay with the
building design as proposed to the Planning Commission which includes an
enclosed, secure playground to provide safety measures for the children. Mr.
Schroeder stated there are questions regarding the street network within the
development but they are unable to modify the plan due to topography
limitations. He stated they will agree to connect the pedestrian walkways to
adjoin with the other parcels when St. Elizabeth completes their development.
Mayor Reinersman suggested they go ahead and extend the sidewalks now and then
St. Elizabeth would need to tie in. Another issue is the parking which Ms.
Ballard does not want shared parking with the other buildings due to security
issues for the daycare children. Mr. Schroeder stated the amenities in this
zone require signage plans which they have not yet submitted. He said they will
need to acquire land from the State of Kentucky for sign placement. He stated
they will pursue this acquisition with the State and signage will be installed
as soon as possible. He stated Ms. Ballard will also agree to an additional
amenity of an exterior bench. Mr. Schroeder advised the GMU zone requires at
least 40% transparency for all customer entrance walls. He stated Ms. Ballard
will agree to this condition. Mr. Schroeder also advised the load/unloading
area will be increased to meet the zone requirements.
Mayor Reinersman questioned the materials that would be used for the exterior
of the building – manufactured versus natural. He stated the GMU zone requires
the exterior materials be wood, stone, brick or a composite of similar style.
Mr. Schroeder commented that some composite materials are permitted in the GMU
zone with the natural materials.
Council Member Franzen asked if this development plan had a public hearing by
the Planning Commission (PDS). Mr. Gatlin advised that a unique feature of this
GMU zone is that final approval on the conditions would be made the City
Council, but PDS staff has advised that the proposed Stage II development plan
does not meet the GMU guidelines. Council Member Franzen asked if Ms. Ballard
was advised of this before she purchased the lot from Arlinghaus. Mayor
Reinersman stated he spoke with both Ms. Ballard and Mr. Schroeder and told
them he did not think this would meet the zone guidelines as well. Mr.
Schroeder stated he advised Ms. Ballard that this parcel was in a special zone
(GMU) but she has not been through this process before now and was not aware of
the conditions that would be imposed. Mr. Schroeder commented that a daycare is
a permitted use in this zone but that the GMU zone requires a unique process
which provides Council the opportunity to approve or disapprove specific
conditions.
Mr. Gatlin advised Council they have three options before them: 1) approve as
submitted; 2) approve with conditions; or 3) reject the proposed plan and then
Ms. Ballard will go back to the drawing board and present a different plan.
Council Member Franzen asked if a revised plan would go back to PDS for review.
He advised the revised plan would not go back to PDS, it would come back to
Council for review and approval/disapproval. He stated this was a unique
process that was set up when the zone was established – Council wanted final
say on this particular zone.
Council Member Aseere asked how many employees would be hired and if they would
close the other location in the Cherokee Plaza. Ms. Ballard stated they would
employ 30-40 full time employees and will continue some classes at the Cherokee
Plaza location.
Mr. Schroeder advised the lightning and landscape plans will be similar to the
St. Elizabeth medical building and will be designed to meet the requirements of
the zone. In closing, Mr. Schroeder stated that in reviewing the requirements
of the zone he believes the proposed development plan for this daycare building
meets the guidelines of the GMU zone.
Mr. Gatlin reviewed the guidelines discussed which included extending the
walkways, revising the windows to provide 40% transparency, revise the load/
unloading area and adding a minor amenity of a bench. He stated compliance with
these conditions would meet the intent of the zone.
Mayor Reinersman spoke about the intent of this mixed use zone (GMU). He stated
this zone is the gateway into the City and was intended as a unique zone to set
it apart from the other zones in the City. He stated ideally the façade of the
buildings would look like multiple buildings resembling a row of main street
shops. He stated he understands the problem of security for the daycare in
shared parking with the other buildings in the development, but that the
daycare should meet the zone requirements, not the other way around. Mayor
Reinersman advised this is not a question about the permitted use but the
vision of this zone. He stated a committee spent eighteen (18) months on the
process of establishing the guidelines of this zone to provide for a
distinctive gateway to the City without making it too restrictive and it
received unanimous approval by the City Council. Mr. Schroeder stated the
building materials for the exterior do meet the zone requirements and he feels
it is a nice design. He stated the fence along the rear play area will
complement the area and reiterated that a daycare is a permitted use in this
zone and in his opinion the development plan meets the requirements of the
zone.
Council Member Franzen asked PDS Senior Planner Andy Videkovich how they could
meet the intent of the zone. Mr. Videkovich advised it is not the use, but the
design and layout of the building that is not consistent with the GMU zone. A
discussion ensued regarding the design of the daycare building in this
development. Mayor Reinersman commented that the St. Elizabeth medical building
is not visible from the street so the proposed building doesn’t have to match
that building. Council Member Franzen commented that while she is not opposed
to the proposed building design, it may become a precedent that will be hard to
break. Council Member Brinker asked Mr. Schroeder how many lots were in this
development. Mr. Schroeder advised there are a total of eight acres, only six
of which are buildable, for a total of five building parcels. Mayor Reinersman
advised the entire GMU zone encompasses a total of forty acres.
Council Member Aseere suggested tabling action on this Stage II Development
Plan until the September meeting and until a common ground could be determined.
Council Member Franzen so moved, seconded by Council Member Aseere. Roll call
was answered unanimously. Motion carried 5-0.
Proposed Ordinance – Approving a Zoning Text Amendment Adding “Single Family
Residential Dwellings (attached)” as a Permitted Use Within the R-2 Zone – 1st
Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a first reading a proposed ordinance

that would rename a portion of Centennial Boulevard that intersects with
Declaration Drive and Madison Pike to “Richard Wainscott Way.” Mr. Gatlin gave
the proposed ordinance a first reading.
Proposed Ordinance – Authorizing Delinquent Fowler Creek Sewer Assessments to
be Added to the Annual Tax Bill – 1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a first reading a proposed ordinance
that would stop the Fowler Creek Sewer Assessment and provide for the placement
of the delinquent assessments on the City ad valorem tax bill and would repeal
Ordinance No. 2012-O-02 that deals with the collection of unpaid assessments.
Mr. Gatlin gave the proposed ordinance a first reading.
Mr. Gatlin advised this ordinance will allow the City to directly place the
delinquent assessment accounts on the annual property tax bill for future
notice and collection of the unpaid assessments. He stated he has provided the
Mayor a letter of his legal opinion regarding the placement of this assessment
delinquency on the tax bills.

Award Bids for the Purchase of a Ford 550 Dump Truck for the Public Services
Department
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council one bid that was received from Fuller
Ford for the purchase of a 550 Series, four wheel drive dump truck in the
amount of $69,350.00. Mr. Moriconi advised this bid amount is in line with the
budgeted funds and the truck is the same style that has been purchased in the
past. He stated the Public Services Director likes this truck model in terms of
power and transmission. He stated he hopes to get the truck ordered and
delivered in November in time for snow removal months.
A motion was made by Council Member Franzen and seconded by Council Member
Yeager to award the bid to Fuller Ford in the amount of $69,350.00. Roll was
called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 5-0.
Resolution No. 2015-R-14 - Memorandum of Agreement for the Northern Kentucky
Regional Hazard Mitigation Plan
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Resolution No. 2015-R-14 that would
approve a Memorandum of Agreement for participation in the Northern Kentucky
Regional Hazard Mitigation Planning. Mr. Gatlin read Resolution No. 2015-R-14.
A motion was made by Council Member Franzen and seconded by Council Member
Brinker to approve Resolution No. 2015-R-14. Roll was called and answered
unanimously. Motion carried 5-0.
Attorney’s Report – Jack Gatlin
Mr. Gatlin stated his first forty days on the job as the City’s attorney has
been a pleasure. He reported that he has entered appearances in all the City’s
bank foreclosure cases and advised there are forty-nine (49) active cases which
he will be monitoring.
City Administrator Report – Chris Moriconi
Mr. Moriconi updated Council on the Pelly Road Bridge closing. He advised they
met with the engineers from the Transportation Cabinet’s District 6 office to
discuss options for the bridge repair. He stated the City has been awarded
$56,700 in emergency road aid from the State to help offset the repair costs.
He hopes to have more updates at the September meeting.
Mr. Moriconi also reported the Kenton County driver’s license testing office in
the rear of the old Kroger building officially opens for business tomorrow.
Council Member Yeager asked if the City has received word on the award of the
grant application for amphitheater project. Mr. Moriconi responded that he
expects to hear something by September or October.
Mayor’s Report – Christopher J. Reinersman
Mayor Reinersman thanked everyone that helped make the annual Independence Day
Celebration a great success again this year. He expressed his sadness at the
passing of Vito Casullo whose fireworks display each year was the highlight of
the two-day event. He also thanked all the sponsors, and especially thanked
Council Member Yeager for soliciting the sponsors who contribute to the
fireworks show each year.
Proclamation – World Overdose Prevention Day – Mayor Reinersman stated the
Heroin Drug Task Force has approached all the cities in Northern Kentucky to
proclaim August 31, 2015 as Overdose Prevention Day in Independence. He read
the Proclamation. A motion was made by Council Member Yeager and seconded by
Council Member Aseere in favor of the Proclamation. The motion carried with all
ayes.
Adjournment
There being no further business, a motion was made by Council Member Yeager and
seconded by Council Member Deaton to adjourn. Motion carried with all ayes and
the meeting ended at 8:25 p.m.

SPECIAL COUNCIL MEETING
August 24, 2015
Opening
The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met in a special session
on Monday, August 24, 2015 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the
Independence Municipal Center, 5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with
Mayor Christopher Reinersman presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to
order and opened with the Pledge of Allegiance. Roll was called and the
following Council Members registered present: Bill Aseere, Tom Brinker, Jim
Bushong, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and Donna Yeager. Also present was City
Administrator Chris Moriconi, City Attorney Jack Gatlin and City Clerk Patricia
Taney.
Purpose of the Special Meeting
Mayor Reinersman announced this Special meeting of Council was being held to
discuss and take action on the following business items:
1.   Introduction of Mike Carpenter as the City’s new Building Inspector
2.   Municipal Order No. 2015-MO-02 - Appointment of a City Representative to
the County Joint Code Enforcement Board
3.   Ordinance No. 2015-O-15 – Approving Street Name Change from Centennial
Blvd. to Richard Wainscott Way – 2nd Reading
4.   Ordinance No. 2015-O-16 – Approving a Zoning Text Amendment Adding “Single
Family Residential Dwellings (attached)” as a Permitted Use Within the R-2 Zone
– 2nd Reading
5.   Resolution 2015-R-12 - Approval of Stage II Development Plan in GMU Zone
6.   Proposed Ordinance – Adopting 2015 Property Tax Rates – 1st Reading
7.   Proposed Ordinance – Establishing for Bid a Non-Exclusive Natural Gas
Franchise for the placement of Facilities Within the Public Right-of-Way of the
City – 1st Reading
8.   Proposed Ordinance – Establishing for Bid a Non-Exclusive Electric
Franchise for the Placement of Facilities of Electrical Energy within the
Public Right-of-Way of the City – 1st Reading
9.   Proposed Ordinance – Establishing the Authority of the Kenton County
Unified Code Enforcement Board and Amending the City Code of Ordinances
Regarding Nuisances and Classification of Certain Offenses as Civil Offenses –
1st Reading
10.   Proposed Ordinance – Repealing Ordinance No. 2004-O-14 and Adopting the
2012 International Property Maintenance Code and Providing for the Issuance of
Permits and Collection of Fees – 1st Reading
11.   Authorizing an Extension of Agreement with Ernst Concrete
12.   Executive Session (if necessary)
Mayor Reinersman advised that only the items listed on this agenda would be
discussed at this meeting.
Mayor Reinersman made a request to move the last agenda item, authorizing an
Extension of the Agreement with Ernst Concrete to the second agenda item.
Council Member Brinker so moved, seconded by Council Member Yeager. Motion
carried with all ayes.
Introduction of Mike Carpenter as the City’s new Building Inspector
Mayor Reinersman introduced Mike Carpenter to Council as the City’s new
Building Inspector. He stated that Mike is a resident of Independence and has a
long history as a Building Inspector.
Mr. Carpenter gave a brief overview of building permits issued last year,
saying that at this time last year 80 permits had been issued versus 74 permits
issued so far this year. A total of 324 building permits were issued in 2014
and this year the total is currently at 281. He stated total fees collected
last year were $190,000 compared to $187,000 collected to date for 2015.
Mr. Carpenter stated he is happy to be the Building Inspector for Independence
and has been staying busy with all the development in the City.
Council Member Bushong asked Mr. Carpenter about his background and experience.
Mr. Carpenter advised he is a 1997 graduate of Northern Kentucky University and
worked in the private sector before working at PDS (Planning and Development
Services of NKY) for fourteen years and most recently spent two years as
Campbell County’s Building Inspector.
Council Member Brinker asked if Mr. Carpenter would be doing commercial
building inspections as well as residential. Mr. Carpenter stated that while he
has the qualifications to perform those inspection the Planning Commission
(PDS) would continue to inspect the State level buildings for now.
Authorizing an Extension of Agreement with Ernst Concrete
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council an amended price quote from Ernst
Concrete that would extend the current contract with them to furnish ready mix
concrete for the various projects handled by the Public Services Department. He
stated the current contract permits an extension/renewal for three one-year
periods.
Hearing no comments from Council, Mayor Reinersman asked for a motion to
approve. So moved by Council Member Yeager and seconded by Council member
Franzen. Roll was called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Municipal Order No. 2015-MO-02 - Appointment of a City Representative to the
Kenton County Joint Code Enforcement Board
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Municipal Order No. 2015-MO-02 that would
appoint Greg Waite to the Kenton County Joint Code Enforcement Board. He
advised that the City’s current representative on this Board, Catherine Wilson,
has taken a job transfer out of State and has resigned from the Board. He
stated that Greg Waite is a retired firefighter from the Independence Fire
District and he feels he will be a good representative for the City on this
Code Enforcement Board.
A motion was made by Council Member Bushong and seconded by Council Member
Aseere to adopt Municipal Order 2015-MO-02 appointing Greg Waite to the Kenton
County Joint Code Enforcement Board. Roll was called and answered unanimously.
Motion carried 6-0.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-15 – Approving Street Name Change from Centennial Blvd. to
Richard Wainscott Way – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-15, an ordinance that would rename a portion of Centennial Boulevard that
intersects with Declaration Drive and Madison Pike to “Richard Wainscott Way.”
Mr. Gatlin read Ordinance No. 2015-O-15.
A motion was made by Council Member Franzen and seconded by Council Member
Bushong to adopt Ordinance No. 2015-R-15. Roll was called and answered
unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-16 – Approving a Zoning Text Amendment Adding “Single
Family Residential Dwellings (attached)” as a Permitted Use Within the R-2 Zone
– 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-16 that would amend the zoning ordinance adding single family residential
dwellings (attached) as a permitted use within the R-2 Zone. Mr. Gatlin read
Ordinance No. 2015-O-16.
A motion was made by Council Member Yeager and seconded by Council Member
Brinker to adopt Ordinance No. 2015-R-16. Roll was called and answered
unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Resolution 2015-R-12 - Approval of Stage II Development Plan in GMU Zone
Mayor Reinersman re-introduced Resolution No. 2015-R-12 which was tabled at the
August 3rd meeting to provide more time to iron out the conditions that would
need to be met by the property owner to comply with approval of this Stage II
Development Plan in the GMU zone located in the Courthouse Crossing development
at the corner of McCullum and New SR17.
Mr. Bob Schroeder of Arlinghaus Builders who is the Courthouse Crossing
developer stated that he understands and is in agreement with the conditions
and changes made to the exterior design. Joe Brumback of B.L. Spille
Construction stated that the asphalt products used for the project will meet or
exceed the requirements for this zone. A brief discussion ensued regarding the
redesign of the building exterior to meet the 40% transparency requirement with
Mr. Schroeder agreeing to note the types of materials that would be used on the
revised plan.
Council Member Franzen read a prepared statement wherein she voiced her
opposition to approving this Stage II Development Plan. She feels that the
property owner (Jessica Ballard) was advised of the intent of the GMU zone
prior to purchasing the property, then designed the building concept that did
not fit the intent of the zone. Council Member Franzen went on to say that as
part of the Small Area Study, a Committee was formed and the members were
assigned the task of creating new zones for the downtown and gateway areas. She
stated a lot of Committee time and money was spend to implement the final
product. She stated she feels strongly that if the Council votes to approve
this that the City would be going against the plan intended for the GMU zone.
She stated that more is expected in this zone and the intent should be honored
and the decision to approve this Stage II plan should be based on the intent.
Council Member Yeager commented that the St. Elizabeth medical building that
was approved and built there did not fit the intent of the GMU zone either.
Mayor Reinersman commented that the Planning Commission staff recommendation
was to disapprove this plan.
Council Member Yeager moved to approve Resolution No. 2015-R-12 that would
authorize the Stage II Development Plan for the approximate 1.9 acre area
located at 155 Courthouse Crossing for the Kentucky Learning Center. The motion
was seconded by Council Member Aseere.
Further discussion ensued. Council Member Deaton commented that he has read the
Small Area Study and feels the City should honor the Study, but feels it is
hard to stop business growth with a Plan that was basically adopted ten years
ago. He stated both have legitimate weight but the City needs to be flexible
and not punish future business growth for mistakes that may have been made in
the past. Council Member Franzen reiterated the process in developing these new
zones was a long undertaking by the Committee and the City invested in the
Study that should not be put on the shelf and never implemented. Council Member
Aseere commented that the City should be flexible with the businesses and that
government should not get in the way of entrepreneurs.
At this time roll was called on Council Member Yeager’s motion and answered
with five ayes and one no cast by Council Member Franzen.
Mr. Gatlin re-read Resolution No. 2015-R-12 which included the following agreed
upon conditions for approval of the Stage II Development Plan for an
approximate 1.9 acre area located at 155 Courthouse Crossing:
1.   Sidewalk connectors to other parcels pursuant to staff approval and
recommendation
2.   Landscaping Plan pursuant to staff approval and recommendation
3.   Lighting Plan pursuant to staff approval and recommendation
4.   Minimal amenities to include a decorative bench
5.   Final asphalt specifications will meet or exceed staff recommendation
6.   Drawings and specifications for rear elevation pursuant to the attached
Exhibit “A” and including as materials: hardiplank siding, brick and split
faced block
7.   Final Plan will meet or exceed transparency requirements for GMU zone and
subject to staff approval and recommendation
Mr. Gatlin requested Council re-affirm approval of Resolution No. 2015-R-12
with a motion and vote. Council Member Yeager so moved with second by Council
Member Aseere. Roll was called and answered with five ayes and one no vote cast
by Council Member Franzen. Motion carried 5-1.
Proposed Ordinance – Adopting 2015 Property Tax Rates – 1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman submitted for a first reading a proposed ordinance that would
adopt the real estate and personal property tax rates for 2015. Mr. Gatlin read
the proposed ordinance that would adopt the compensating tax rates that have
been calculated at $0.254/$100 assessed value for real estate property and
$0.642/$100 assessed value for personal property.
Proposed Ordinance – Establishing for Bid a Non-Exclusive Natural Gas Franchise
for the placement of Facilities Within the Public Right-of-Way of the City –
1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a first reading a proposed ordinance
that would create and establish for bid a non-exclusive natural gas franchise
for the placement of facilities for transmission, distribution and sale of
natural gas within the public right-of-way of the City for a ten (10) year
duration and reserving the right to impose a franchise fee in the sum of up to
five percent (5%) of gross receipts per year. Mr. Gatlin gave the proposed
ordinance a first reading.
Proposed Ordinance – Establishing for Bid a Non-Exclusive Electric Franchise
for the Placement of Facilities of Electrical Energy within the Public Right-
of-Way of the City – 1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a first reading a proposed ordinance
that would create and establish for bid a non-exclusive electric franchise for
the placement of facilities for the transmission, distribution and sale of
electrical energy within the public right-of-way of the City for a ten (10)
year duration reserving the right to impose a franchise fee in the sum of up to
five percent (5%) of gross receipts per year. Mr. Gatlin gave the proposed
ordinance a first reading.
Proposed Ordinance – Establishing the Authority of the Kenton County Unified
Code Enforcement Board and Amending the City Code of Ordinances Regarding
Nuisances and Classification of Certain Offenses as Civil Offenses – 1st
Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a first reading a proposed ordinance
that would establish the authority of the Kenton County Joint Code Enforcement
Board and amend the City’s Code of Ordinances regarding nuisances and
classification of certain offenses as civil offenses. He explained this
amendment is basically a housekeeping issue to give more power to the Code
Enforcement Officer and Board. Mr. Gatlin read the proposed ordinance and
advised Council that additionally this revision will provide that being found
guilty of a violation will be a civil offense rather than a misdemeanor thereby
keeping this in-house to be handled under the authority of the Joint Code
Enforcement Board.
Council Member Deaton asked if the other cities handled this similarly. Mr.
Gatlin replied yes and it will give the cities more power to keep it at the
Code Enforcement level rather than going through the court system.
Council Member Brinker asked about Section II (C) relating to a person that is
served but does not abate the nuisance within the time frame. Mr. Gatlin stated
this would allow the City to cut the grass, etc. and recoup the City’s cost to
do so thereby strengthening enforcement.
Proposed Ordinance – Repealing Ordinance No. 2004-O-14 and Adopting the 2012
International Property Maintenance Code and Providing for the Issuance of
Permits and Collection of Fees – 1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a first reading a proposed ordinance
that would repeal Ordinance No. 2004-O-14 which adopted the 2003 International
Property maintenance Code and adopt the 2012 International Property Maintenance
Code and all subsequent amendments and future editions thereto. Mr. Gatlin gave
the proposed ordinance a first reading.
Adjournment
There being no further business, a motion was made by Council Member Brinker
and seconded by Council Member Yeager to adjourn. Motion carried with all ayes
and the meeting ended at 7:43 p.m.
