COUNCIL MEETING
September 14, 2015
Opening
The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, September
14, 2015 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal
Center, 5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher
Reinersman presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened
with the Pledge of Allegiance and Council Member Bushong gave the invocation.
Mayor Reinersman asked for a moment of silence out of respect for all police
officers especially fallen Kentucky State Officer Joseph Ponder who was shot
and killed while conducting a traffic stop on Sunday. Roll was called and the
following Council Members registered present: Bill Aseere, Tom Brinker, Jim
Bushong, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and Donna Yeager. Also present was City
Administrator Chris Moriconi, City Clerk Patricia Taney and Attorney Tim Spille
who was filling in for his associate, City Attorney Jack Gatlin.
Approval of the August 3, 2015 Regular Meeting Minutes
Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve the minutes of the regular
meeting held on Monday, August 3, 2015. Council Member Franzen so moved, with
second by Council Member Brinker. No amendments to the minutes were noted, roll
was called and answered with five ayes and one abstain from Council Member
Bushong. Motion carried 5-1.
Approval of the August 24, 2015 Special Meeting Minutes
Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve the minutes of the special
meeting held on Monday, August 24, 2015. Council Member Bushong so moved, with
second by Council Member Franzen. No amendments to the minutes were noted, roll
was called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Resolution No. 2015-R-15 – Approving an Interlocal Agreement Creating the
Florence, Erlanger, Elsmere and Independence Unified Police Protection System &
Authorizing the Mayor to Sign all Relevant Documents
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Resolution No. 2015-R-15 that would
approve joining an Interlocal agreement with the cities of Florence, Erlanger
and Elsmere to create a unified police protection system and authorize the
mayor to sign all the relevant documents. Mr. Spille read Resolution No. 2015-
R-15.
Mayor Reinersman advised Council that Chief Lucas had learned of this
Interlocal agreement between Florence, Erlanger and Elsmere that created full
policing powers across jurisdictional lines of those cities and felt this would
be good for Independence as well as it would create an added layer of
protection for our citizens. He stated that many of the police officers may
live in one city and work in the other so this will allow them to have
authority in both cities going to and from work.
Resolution No. 2015-R-16 – PDS Agreement to Add another Level of Service
Relating to Nuisance Issues
Mayor Reinersman advised Council that he would like to remove Resolution No.
2015-R-16 from the agenda as he has some concerns about making the jump from
Service Level 2 to Service Level 4 specifically with regard to the higher fee
structure. The City currently pays 25% of PDS’ actual costs and advancing to
Level 4 would require the City to pay 75% of PDS’ actual costs for Level 4. He
stated that PDS Executive Director Dennis Gordon was out of town, so he was
unable to discuss them increase in the fee schedule. He stated he would like to
scratch this agenda item and will consider placing it on the October 5th
meeting agenda after he discusses this with Mr. Gordon.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-17 – Adopting 2015 Property Tax Rates – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-17 that would adopt the real estate and personal property tax rates for 2015.
Mr. Spille gave Ordinance No. 2015-O-17 a second reading to adopt the
compensating tax rates that have been calculated at $0.254/$100 assessed value
for real estate property and $0.642/$100 assessed value for personal property.
Council Member Bushong moved to adopt Ordinance No. 2015-O-17 with a second by
Council Member Yeager. There being no discussion, roll was called and answered
unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-18 – Establishing for Bid a Non-Exclusive Natural Gas
Franchise for the placement of Facilities Within the Public Right-of-Way of the
City – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-18 that would create and establish for bid a non-exclusive natural gas
franchise for the placement of facilities for transmission, distribution and
sale of natural gas within the public right-of-way of the City for a ten (10)
year duration and reserving the right to impose a franchise fee in the sum of
up to five percent (5%) of gross receipts per year. Mr. Spille gave Ordinance
No. 2015-O-18 a second reading.

Regarding Nuisances and Classification of Certain Offenses as Civil Offenses –
2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-20 that would establish the authority of the Kenton County Joint Code
Enforcement Board and also amend the City’s Code of Ordinances regarding
nuisances and classification of certain offenses as civil offenses. He
explained this amendment is basically a housekeeping issue to reclassify
certain offenses as civil, not a misdemeanor, thereby making the civil offenses
subject to the jurisdiction of the Joint Code Enforcement Board for quicker

Mayor Reinersman introduced Tim Spille, associate of City Attorney Jack Gatlin,

made a few comments and advised he did not have a formal report to present.
City Administrator Report – Chris Moriconi
Mr. Moriconi updated Council on the Pelly Road Bridge closing. He advised they
have been in on-going discussions with the engineers and is hopeful he will
have a more tangible plan for repairs to the bridge in the coming weeks.
Mayor’s Report – Christopher J. Reinersman
Pelly Road Bridge Discussion - Mayor Reinersman reported he was invited to
speak to a third grade class at Summit View Academy and was even questioned
about the Pelly Road Bridge by one of the students. Council Member Bushong
asked what steps could be taken to prevent repeat damage by trucks in the
future. Mayor Reinersman stated the City Engineer suggested a concrete wall
that would be attached to the southern box beam, instead of a guardrail. This
should prevent trucks from knocking it off. Additionally, he feels an ordinance
prohibiting trucks on this section of roadway may be necessary. In response to
Council Member Deaton’s question, Mayor Reinersman stated they have confirmed
that truckers are getting GPS routing directions to Pelly Road. He stated they
are attempting to contact these companies to request they provide alternate
routes. Council Member Yeager asked if consideration was being given to close
Pelly Road to through traffic and install a school bus turn-around. Mayor
Reinersman advised the City Engineer is confident that the wall option will be
a good fix at $250,000. He stated the City received $57,000 in State Emergency
Municipal Road Aid which was based on an $80,000 repair cost, but with a new
$250,000 repair estimate, the City may have to go back to the State and request
more emergency funding. Mayor Reinersman stated a bridge replacement that would
include abutments would run around $820,000. Mr. Moriconi advised that the
$250,000 repair estimate takes the surface and to reconfigure the intersection
entirely would be well over a million dollar project. Mayor Reinersman advised
it would be a multimillion project to build a new bridge and realign the
intersection. He stated a repair cost of $250,000 would include an additional
box beam and that the City will continue to look for the funds to make these
repairs.
Mayor Reinersman that he, along with Council Member Bushong, attended the
Northern Kentucky 911 Memorial dedication ceremony in Crescent Springs where
the memorial is located. He stated it was an impressive ceremony and they had a
good turnout.
Mayor Reinersman encouraged everyone to attend the Kenton County Farm Harvest
Tour this Saturday. He stated more information about the Tour can be found on
the City Facebook page and there are brochures in the lobby.
Mayor Reinersman stated that this year’s annual Christmas Walk will be held on
Saturday, December 5th. He stated a new event this year will be a 5K Santa Run
on Saturday afternoon.
Adjournment
There being no further business, a motion was made by Council Member Franzen
and seconded by Council Member Yeager to adjourn. Motion carried with all ayes
and the meeting ended at 7:22 p.m.

COUNCIL MEETING
November 9, 2015
Opening
The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, November
8, 2015 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal
Center, 5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher
Reinersman presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened
with the Pledge of Allegiance and Council Member Bushong gave the invocation.
Roll was called and the following Council Members registered present: Tom
Brinker, Jim Bushong, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and Donna Yeager. Also
present was City Administrator Chris Moriconi, City Clerk Patricia Taney and
City Attorney Jack Gatlin. Council Member Bill Aseere was absent.
Approval of the October 5, 2015 Regular Meeting Minutes
Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve the minutes of the regular
meeting held on October 5, 2015. Council Member Yeager so moved, with a second
by Council Member Franzen. No amendment to the minutes were noted, roll was
called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 5-0.
Discussion relating to a Stage II Development Plan for a Daycare at 146
McCullum Road (Hofstetter property)
Mayor Reinersman began the discussion for possible action for a proposed
daycare development at 146 McCullum Road. Mr. Wallace Boggs law firm Attorney
Bill Boggs, who represents the Littlest Angels and LA Properties, addressed
council. Bill Boggs stated that the Littlest Angels Daycare will fit into the
GMU zone requirements including green space, walkable environments, social
interaction, outdoor activities, creating a sense of space and a walkable
environment.
Carrie DePue, Director and owner of Littlest Angels Daycare in Union, Kentucky,
stated the proposed daycare would not be a commercial type center but more of a
residential type center. The center will provide an extended family setting and
will include a playground, green space with walking trail and fencing for
security. She also stated that the daycare would offer space for the kids to go
outside to have relay races, play soccer, build snowmen, nature walks, all of
which cannot be found at the typical commercial type centers. Council asked
about the staff size of the proposed center and Ms. DePue stated that her staff
at the Union facility is currently between 23 and 28 and that she would expect
to have similar staffing levels for the proposed Independence center when the
three phases of construction are complete.
Mayor Reinersman stated the Planning and Development Services (PDS) has
recommended disapproval of the proposed plan, citing eleven conditions that do
not meet the Gateway Mixed Use (GMU) zone requirements. Council Member Franzen
stated that she didn’t think that the 40% transparency should apply for this
building. Council Member Deaton commented this daycare proposal should be held
to the same requirements that were asked of the previous daycare proposal and
should have a similar agreement. Bill Boggs addressed some of the issues PDS
commented on in their recommendation for disapproval of the Plan. He stated
construction materials would consist of hardy board siding; they will comply
with lighting requirements; the driveway measurements have been updated for
compliance and they would supply/comply with signage regulations. Council
Member Brinker stated that he would like to see drawings of the proposed
building as well as responses to all eleven items that PDS outlined in their
recommendation before he would be comfortable with approving the proposed
development plan.
Council Member Yeager moved to approve the proposed Stage II development plan
contingent upon completing the eleven conditions as recommended by PDS. A
second was made by Council Member Deaton. Roll was called and the answered with
two ayes cast by Council Members Yeager and Deaton and three nays cast by
Council Members Brinker, Bushong and Franzen. Motion failed 2-3.
Mayor Reinersman suggested the developer/owner make revisions to the
development plan and address the Council at the December 7th meeting. He
advised they come back with pictures of the current building on the site and
renderings of the planned modifications to that structure, a good site plan,
blueprints, elevation plan, lighting plan and signage drawings to specifically
address each of the eleven conditions of the GMU zone.
Proposed Ordinance – Intent to Annex
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council a proposed ordinance to annex three
parcels in unincorporated Kenton County located along Madison Pike and north of
Patriot Way. He advised Council the City was contacted by O’Reilly Auto Parts
who expressed interest in building a store on the one vacant parcel. He stated
this area along Madison Pike has an odd shape island that is unincorporated and
since it receives City services he felt the City should probably consider
annexing the area. He stated since one of the vacant parcels is owned by the
Kenton County Fiscal Court he contacted the County to let them know of the
City’s intention to annex the area and they stated they would not object to the
annexation. The other two parcels include another vacant lot and the Dollar
General Store lot. Mr. Gatlin gave the proposed ordinance a first reading.
Mayor Reinersman advised the City Clerk would send notice to the property
owners of the City’s intent to annex the parcels.
Resolution No. 2015-R-18 – Authorizing a Zoning Text Amendment Application
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Resolution No. 2015-R-18 authorizing a
zoning text amendment application to amend the language of a Neighborhood
Commercial (NC) zone to allow that an “automotive parts and accessories” store
would be considered as a permitted us. He stated this added use to the NC zone
is in anticipation of the O’Reilly Auto Parts store locating on the site the
City is proposing to annex. Mr. Gatlin gave the proposed ordinance a first
reading.
Council Member Franzen moved to approve Resolution No. 2015-R-18, seconded by
Council Member Bushong. Roll was called and answered unanimously. Motion
carried 5-0.
Municipal Order No. 2015-O-03 – Adopting the “Independence Complete Streets
Policy”
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council a Municipal Order No. 2015-O-03 for the
adoption of the Complete Streets Policy for the city. He introduced Kelly
Schwegman of the Northern Kentucky Health Department who gave a PowerPoint
presentation that provided a detailed explanation of a Complete Streets Policy
that sets forth guiding principles and practices for public transportation
projects to encourage walking, bicycling and other non-motorized forms of
transit to encourage being physically active. Elements would include bike
lanes, sidewalks, crosswalks, pedestrian signs, etc. Ms. Schwegman discussed
the benefits of Complete Streets which are: improved safety, increased physical
activity, improved air quality, safer routes to school, etc. The Mayor advised
Council that, when practical and economical, the City could apply some of these
guidelines. He stated that by adopting this policy now it would give the City
options to address when doing future projects. He went on to say this is
considered a long term policy and the City would not be committed to
implementing these guideline features right away. In addition, the Mayor stated
that by adopting this policy, it may increase grant approvals for the City
through OKI and will not cost the city anything to adopt this Policy.
After a brief question and answer period and there being no further discussion,
Council Member Franzen moved to adopt Municipal Order No. 2015-MO-03, with a
second by Council Member Brinker. Roll was called and answered with three ayes
cast by Council members Franzen, Brinker and Bushong and two no votes cast by
Council Members Yeager and Deaton. Motion carried 3-2.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-22 - Award Electric Franchise to Owen Electric – 2nd
Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-22 for the award of a non-exclusive electric energy franchise for the term of
ten years to Owen Electric. Mr. Gatlin gave Ordinance No. 2015-O-22 a second
reading. Council Member Bushong asked how much revenue these franchise fees
would generate for the City and if the Mayor had specific uses for this
revenue. Mayor Reinersman stated that by implementing electric and gas
franchise fees it is anticipated the City will generate about $300,000 in
annual revenue. He advised there are many needs for Police Department, Public
Services Department and Parks that this revenue will benefit. He cited the
needed repairs to the Pelly Road Bridge as an example of a project that would
benefit from this new source of revenue. He stated it recently came to his
attention these franchise fees were in place at one time but in recent years
the franchise agreement/fees had expired, so this legislation will re-instate
those fees and be a source of much needed revenue.
There being no further discussion, a motion was made by Council Member Deaton
to adopt Ordinance No. 2015-O-22 and seconded by Council Member Bushong. Roll
was called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 5-0.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-23 – Award Electric Franchise to Duke Energy – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-23 for the award of a non-exclusive electric energy franchise for the term of
ten years to Duke Energy. Mr. Gatlin gave Ordinance No. 2015-O-23 a second
reading.
A motion was made by Council Member Franzen to adopt Ordinance No. 2015-O-23
and seconded by Council Member Deaton. Roll was called and answered
unanimously. Motion carried 5-0.
Ordinance No. 2015-O-24 – Award Gas Franchise to Duke Energy -2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council for a second reading Ordinance No. 2015-
O-24 for the award of a non-exclusive gas franchise for the term of ten years
to Duke Energy. Mr. Gatlin gave Ordinance No. 2015-O-24 a second reading.
A motion was made by Council Member Bushong and seconded by Council Member
Franzen to approve Ordinance No. 2015-O-24. Roll was called and answered

Mr. Moriconi updated Council on Pelly Road Bridge. He stated that he received

COUNCIL MEETING
December 7, 2015
Opening
The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, December
7, 2015 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal
Center, 5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher
Reinersman presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened
with the Pledge of Allegiance and asked for a moment of silence in lieu of an
invocation. Roll was called and the following Council Members registered
present: Bill Aseere, Tom Brinker, Lucas Deaton and Carol Franzen. Also present
was City Administrator Chris Moriconi, City Clerk Patricia Taney and City
Attorney Jack Gatlin. Council Members Jim Bushong and Donna Yeager were absent.
Approval of the November 9, 2015 Regular Meeting Minutes
Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve the minutes of the regular
meeting held on November 9, 2015. Council Member Franzen so moved, with a
second by Council Member Brinker. No amendments were noted, roll was called and
answered unanimously. Motion carried with 3 ayes and 1 abstain by Council
Member Aseere.
Discussion and Possible Action Relating to a Stage II Development Plan for a
Daycare at 146 McCullum Road (Hofstetter property)
Mayor Reinersman began the discussion regarding a proposed daycare development
at 146 McCullum Road. Mr. Bill Boggs from the law firm of Wallace Boggs, PLLC
representing the Littlest Angels Daycare addressed council. Mr. Boggs stated
that he has provided the Council the additional information they requested at
last month’s meeting as well as a supplement document which contained color
drawings of the proposed development and a mock-up of a sign for the Center.
Mr. Boggs stated that the documents address the eleven issues the Planning
Commission (PDS) raised as well as a plat, survey and pictures to illustrate
each of the proposed changes.
Mr. Jeff Talkers from the civil engineering firm Land Consultants, representing
the Littlest Angels Daycare addressed council. Mr. Talkers presented to Council
illustrations that showed sidewalk infrastructure and the access easement to
adjacent properties. He stated that they prefer not to have two-way traffic to
and from the adjacent properties and suggested one-way traffic accessibility
from the center. Mr. Talkers mentioned that the sidewalk provides a walkway for
children for school bus pickup. He added that the topography is 40 feet above
KY17 and in his opinion, the parcel is not easily graded to create a large
commercial building and so the building would not be visible from KY17. The
sign would be located on the site where it could be visible from KY17.
Andy Videkovich, Principal Planner of Planning and Development Services (PDS),
addressed Council to explain the eleven conditions that did not meet the
Gateway Mixed Use (GMU) zone requirements from last month’s council meeting.
Mr. Videkovich discussed the 40% transparency issue and stated that according
to the ordinance, the daycare is considered a commercial retail sales and
service use and therefore, the transparency requirement would not apply to this
development. He stated it is the PDS staff opinion that the City Council does
not have the authority to waive the transparency requirement. He stated there
are provisions within the GMU zone that would allow Council to modify the
requirement regarding the boulevard entrance if they chose to do so. Mr.
Videkovich commented that the updates to the lighting plan, increasing the two-
way access drive to twenty two feet wide and having the public amenities of
benches and gazebo were satisfactory of the zoning requirements. He stated that
the plans showed enough space to provide loading and unloading to meet the zone
requirement. He mentioned that the access issue to the adjacent property was
addressed by widening the main access drive to 22 feet but added that Council
could approve 11 feet wide as an option for one-way access. Mr. Videkovich
suggested when this development begins Phase 3 and exceeds 7,000 square feet, a
traffic impact study would be necessary to show what the impact would be at
that time. He also added that additional information would be needed when the
building permit application is submitted. He stated that if the land
disturbance is more than one acre they will need to obtain a land disturbance
permit from SD1. Mr. Videkovich added that there are still unanswered questions
and concerns PDS has with regard to this development and whether or not it even
meets the intent of the GMU zone.
There was some discussion from Council regarding the 40% transparency
requirement of the GMU zone and Mr. Videkovich from PDS explained the 40% only
applies to the front of the building. Council Member Deaton questioned if
Council could recommend that the center be required to conduct the traffic
impact study before they being Phase 3 of the development. Council Member
Franzen expressed some concern that Council should be consistent with the same
conditions that were imposed on the previously approved daycare (Kentucky
Learning Center) in the Courthouse Crossing development, particularly the 40%
transparency requirement of the GMU zone.
City Attorney Jack Gatlin provided a recap of the conditions that Council
discussed as follows:
∙   Transparency pursuant to Staff approval and recommendation.
∙   Lighting Plan pursuant to Staff approval and recommendation.
∙   Traffic Study prior to completion of Phase III or prior to any building or
group of buildings exceeding 7500 square feet. The secondary access road may be
required after the Traffic Study.
∙   Signage per Staff approval and recommendation.
∙   Public amenities as proposed and per Staff approval and recommendation.
∙   Sanitary plan per Staff approval and recommendation.
Mr. Gatlin advised he would draft a Resolution authorizing and approving this
development with the above conditions.
There being no further discussion, a motion was made by Council Member Deaton
with a second by Council Member Brinker to approve the development plan, with
conditions stated, for the Littlest Angels Daycare campus located at 146
McCullum Road. Roll was called and answered with three ayes from Council

4, 2016 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal
Center, 5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher
Reinersman presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened
with the Pledge of Allegiance and Council Member Jim Bushong led the
invocation. Roll was called and the following Council Members registered
present: Bill Aseere, Tom Brinker, Jim Bushong, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and
Donna Yeager. Also present was City Administrator Chris Moriconi, City Clerk
Patricia Taney, Assistant City Clerk Gina Gabbard and City Attorney Jack
Gatlin.

Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve Ordinance No. 2016-O-01.
Council Member Franzen so moved with a second by Council Member Brinker. Roll
was called and answered unanimously. Motion carried.
Resolution No. 2016-R-01 – SD1 Laterals
Mayor Reinersman presented Resolution No. 2016-R-01 to Council which would
clarify Sanitation District No. 1’s (SD1) responsibility in regards to lateral
sewer lines on private property. He stated recently, SD1’s position is repairs
to the lateral sewer lines are the responsibility of the property owner. Mayor
Reinersman stated SD1, did at the direction of the three Judge Executives
(Boone, Kenton and Campbell Counties), set aside $600,000 for repairs, but it
is the city’s responsibility for the making repairs to the street after the
sewer lines have been repaired. If cities do not sign the agreement, the
residents/property owners would be responsible for repairs. He stated this
resolution is seeking clarification from SD1 and if passed, would authorize the
Mayor join in the lawsuit on the behalf of Independence residents and let the
court decide who is responsible for the lateral repairs.
Mr. Gatlin explained that SD1’s $600,000 budget was a one-time deal. He added
that $440,000 was previously set aside for exclusively for the City of
Covington before SD1 prior to sending the interlocal agreement to other cities.
He stated the reality is, there was only $160,000 left for the remaining
Northern Kentucky cities. Mr. Gatlin stated the cities that chose not to sign
SD1’s interlocal agreement, SD1 would not service and fix the lateral right-a-
ways in those areas. He stated every City Attorney said it’s illegal and that
cities can’t indemnify SD1 for something such as this. Mr. Gatlin stated the
second issue is cities are required to repair the streets after SD1 repairs the
lateral right-a-ways; and the cost of the street repairs could be more than the
lateral repair. He mentioned the third problem with this proposed agreement
from SD1 is that it is one sided and SD1 could terminate the agreement upon a
thirty day notice. He added it also states the $600,000 budget is for this year
only so it is unknown how this issue will be handled in future years. Mr.
Gatlin stated Erlanger has been dealing with these issues for the past six
months and several cities such as Ft Wright, Park Hills, Cold Spring and
Erlanger have taken formal action to move forward with court action to get a
declaratory judgement. He mentioned there are another five or six cities in
Northern Kentucky that are also in discussions regarding this issue. He stated
cities don’t want to sign this interlocal agreement and feel that clarification
is needed to identify the responsible parties for these lateral lines. Mr.
Gatlin expressed the only way to do this is in the form of a declaratory
judgement to seek guidance from the Kenton Circuit Court. He stated the cities
will take the position that they believe this is SD1’s responsibility and SD1
will take the position that it’s the city’s responsibility and the court will
ultimately decide. He stated the purpose of this resolution is to reach a level
of clarity in Kenton County on who is responsible for the repairs of lateral
right-a-ways. Mr. Gatlin stated by passing this resolution, it is allowing the
Mayor to authorize the law firm to represent the City in seeking a declaratory
judgement from the courts.
Council Member Brinker mentioned he finds it interesting that SD1 determines
their laterals different than electrical providers do their electric lines.
Mayor Reinersman stated he agreed and expressed concern that if this passes,
other utilities could do the same thing. Council Member Franzen stated SD1 is
called Sanitation District for a reason, they maintain sanitation and doesn’t
understand how the lines got blurred. She added it’s almost double dipping for
them, they charge the taxpayer and then the taxes will have to go up because
the city will have to make lateral repairs.
Council Member Deaton asked where the litigation stands as of now. Mr. Gatlin
stated another mayor has suggested each city have their own cap – relative to
their city’s population. Council Member Franzen asked who would be responsible,
as litigation could be a lengthy process. Mayor Reinersman answered, SD1’s
position is it’s the taxpayers’ responsibility; but he hasn’t signed the
interlocal agreement. He stated Erlanger signed the agreement because they had
necessary repairs. He stated Council can discuss this further but if the City
has a problem, we may have to revisit and consider signing the agreement. Mayor
Reinersman stated that Covington has 40-50 sinkholes in their streets, when
sewer lines fail under a street, it eventually collapses and you have residents
that can’t afford $5,000- $15,000 for repair bills for those lateral lines.
Council Member Aseere asked what costs would be associated with the legal
action. Mayor Reinersman stated there is a $3,000 cap for each City joining the
lawsuit. Council Member Aseere also asked if a taxpayer pays for a repair while
litigation is going on, can they come back and be reimbursed from SD1. Mr.
Gatlin stated they are not including the reimbursement idea in the lawsuit but
if the court judgement is in the cities favor and SD1 is determined to be the
responsible party, it could open up separate lawsuits for those cases. Mayor
Reinersman stated he doesn’t see joining this lawsuit as a hostile action
towards SD1, it is just that the cities are looking for clarification on who is
ultimately the responsible party for the repair of the lateral lines. He also
added that it’s not a giant problem currently for Independence but he doesn’t
want to exclude Independence as it could affect the City in the future so being
a part of this process would be in the best interest of the residents. He
stated that if Council agrees to adopt this resolution the City will be a party
to this lawsuit.
There being no further discussion a motion was made by Council Member Aseere to
adopt Resolution No. 2016-R-01 with a second by Council Member Franzen. Roll
was called and answered unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Attorney’s Report – Jack Gatlin
Jack Gatlin stated he will circulate a final draft of the declaratory judgement
action to Council but he is trying to keep it low key as possible. He stated it
should be a legislative fix to this issue.
City Administrator Report – Chris Moriconi
Mr. Moriconi had nothing to report.
Mayor’s Report – Chris Reinersman

Bushong, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and Donna Yeager. Also present was City

Proclamation – Congenital Health Defect Awareness Week – February 7th – 14th,

Mayor Reinersman presented a Proclamation to recognize and the week of February

Approval of the January 4, 2016 Regular Meeting Minutes
Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve the minutes of the regular

by Council Member Bushong. No amendment to the minutes were noted, roll was

Resolution No. 2016-R-02 – Supporting the Implementation of a Needle Exchange
Program to be Administered by the Northern Kentucky Independent District Health
Department from the County Health Centers or St Elizabeth Healthcare Hospitals
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Resolution No. 2016-R-02 which is a
resolution supporting and urging the implementation of a Needle Exchange
Program to be administered by the Northern Kentucky Health District and St.
Elizabeth Healthcare Hospitals. The Mayor stated the issue of increased heroin
use has been a regular topic of the Kenton County Mayors Group as well as a
main concern of the Northern Kentucky Health Department. The Mayor read
statistics from St. Elizabeth Healthcare regarding overdoses: in 2011 there
were 120, in 2012 there were 225, in 2013 there were 285, in 2014 there were
336 and in 2015 there were 565 overdoses. He stated this program gives addicts
the opportunity to not share needles with others, talk to substance abuse
counselors, get tested for diseases and discuss treatment options.
Dr. Lynne Saddler MD, the District Director of Health from the Northern
Kentucky Health Department, presented information about the Needle Exchange
Program. She stated the Northern Kentucky Health Department’s responsibility is
to prevent disease, promote wellness and protect the public against health
threats within Boone, Campbell, Kenton, and Grant counties and is mandated by
KRS 211.180.
Dr. Saddler explained that the increase in IV drug use (particularly heroin)
has led to a rise in:
∙   Drug overdoses and untimely deaths
∙   Emergency room visits and hospitalizations
∙   Babies born to women with drug addiction
∙   Communicable diseases (such as hepatitis C)
∙   Arrests and incarcerations for drug possession, trafficking and other
criminal activity
∙   Impact on businesses and economic development
She also stated the public health is concerned about IV drug use because:
∙   Sharing needles, syringes, and other drug equipment transmits diseases –
hepatitis C, hepatitis B and HIV
∙   Contaminated needles, syringes, and other drug equipment get discarded in
public places which puts the public and first responders at risk for diseases
from accidental needle sticks.
Dr. Saddler advised of several diseases associated with IV drug use which
include:
∙   Hepatitis C – viral infection of the liver, can cause liver failure and/or
death if untreated.
∙   HIV – chronic disease with a lifetime cost of $600,000 for treatment.
∙   Hepatitis B – viral infection of the liver and can become a lifelong
infection.
∙   In the last five years, Hepatitis B rates are up 65%, Hepatitis C rates are
up 120% and HIV rates have not yet increased significantly.
She added Kentucky’s Heroin Law, SB-192, enables local health departments to
operate a needle exchange program with the approval of the city and county in
which the program would operate. The Northern Kentucky District Health
Department’s Board has approved the program but the cities and counties need to
approve before the program can begin.
Dr. Saddler explained the Needle Exchange Program is a comprehensive public
health program to reduce the spread of communicable diseases like Hepatitis C
and B and HIV in a community. The program exchanges sterile syringes, needles
and clean injection equipment for contaminated equipment and properly disposes
of contaminated equipment. She stated the benefits of the program are to help
reduce the spread of diseases and advance public safety for the public, law
enforcement officials and first responders. She added the programs are cost
effective compared to treating HIV and Hepatitis C and for every dollar spent
on the program, will save $7 with the cost of HIV treatment.
Dr. Saddler clarified common misconceptions and myths of these types of
programs by stating that they do not encourage individuals to start using
drugs, does not increase drug use among existing users and does not increase
crime in neighborhoods in which such a program operates.
Mayor Reinersman thanked Dr. Saddler for her presentation and asked Council if
they had any questions. Council Member Franzen asked what percentage of needle
exchange program participants go into treatment, what is the success rate of
completing treatment and if any data was available to indicate these programs
do not bring additional crime to the areas in which these programs operate. Dr.
Saddler stated there are two studies regarding the likelihood of a participant
going to treatment, one says a participant is five times more likely and the
other study says 25% more likely. She did not have stats on the success rates
of the treatment programs. She stated Baltimore did a study and found there was
no additional crime in surrounding areas to the program operation center and in
fact they found a decrease in crime in surrounding areas.
Council Member Aseere questioned the cost to taxpayers for this programs. Dr.
Saddler said the estimated cost is $385 per participant, per year. She added
the Health Department currently offers the testing services to anyone who walks
through the door of the Health Centers and funding is already in place to cover
the costs of those services.
Council Member Franzen asked if the $250,000 funding from the private
foundation is for one year only or if it will be an annual funding and how the
Health Centers will distribute the needles to participants. Dr. Saddler stated
the private foundation funding is secured for one year. She added there are
initial steps for participants but the actual number of needles given is based
on how many times the participant uses and when they anticipate coming back to
the center. Participants will also receive a sharps container to bring back
their next visit and that’s how the exchange begins one for one. She stated St.
Elizabeth Hospital is picking up the cost of the needle disposal.
Council Member Deaton asked if the grants were a local or state wide grant, and
if the goal of this program is to help users lessen their drug usage and go
into treatment. Dr. Saddler stated the private foundation grant is just for the
NKY Health District and the federal funding goes to the state for distribution
between the different health departments. Dr. Sadder clarified the Health
Department’s area of expertise is stopping the spread of diseases but stressed
the importance of having onsite counselors and partnerships with local
treatment centers. She stated this program is only approved to operate at the
NKY Health Department Health Centers, there is not a Health Center in
Independence and this Resolution is supporting the program at the designated
centers in Northern Kentucky. The Mayor commented a needle exchange operation
center couldn’t be set up in Independence unless Council approved an ordinance
to do so. Council Member Deaton commented it is Council’s responsibility to
help protect the police, first responders and the community. He commended Mayor
Reinersman for bringing this to the table as it shows great leadership.
Chief Lucas addressed Council and expressed his support for adopting the
Resolution citing that it’s a safety issue; it helps protect the police, EMTs,
first responders as well as the general public. He stated last year the police
department would touch a heroin incident once a week and this year it has
become a daily occurrence. He stated two years ago, the Health Department came
to train the police and it was the best two hours of training they ever had.
Chief Lucas stated the police officers wore poke proof gloves and need to ask
victims and suspects if they have anything that could poke them.
Alan Daly, 10330 Limerick Circle, Independence – voiced his support of the
needle exchange program. He stated is a good idea for the safety of our troops
but believes there should be specific exchange requirements on how many are
given out against how many are brought in. Dr. Saddler stated the maximum
number would be initially 40 and after 1-2 visits, it should be an even
exchange.
Kevin Napier, 112 Walnut Creek Drive, Independence - a candidate for the House
of Representatives in District 61, voiced his support for the program. He
stated he is the founder of the Kentuckians Against Heroin and has worked with
the Lexington Health Department in implementing their needle exchange program.
He stated he works with the recovery unit and there’s been 12 referrals from
the Lexington Health Department that have successfully completed treatment and
are back into the workforce. In 2015, the Lexington needle exchange program had
199 visits, took in 5,293 and gave out 5,389 which is less than a 100
difference.
Sean Fitzgerald, 2116 Comice Court, Independence - an attorney and candidate
for State Representative in District 64, expressed his concern regarding the
program. He stated he is opposed to the needle exchange because there isn’t a
requirement for all needles to be turned back in. Dr. Saddler stated the
participants are counseled each visit and told to bring back all needles given.
She added the program may not start off one for one but they work towards it.
She also clarified the four NKY Health Centers are in Covington, Newport,
Florence and Williamstown and this resolution is not proposing to open
additional centers. Mr. Fitzgerald stated he found unsuccessful studies of
needle exchange programs in Seattle, San Francisco and Montreal. Dr. Saddler
stated the Seattle’s program was successful with the prevention of increased
HIV rates.
Council Member Aseere questioned who would decide if this program passes. Mayor
Reinersman stated the first step is the Health Department, then Kenton County
has to approve, followed by the cities in which the centers would operate. The
Health Department has already approved it and Kenton County Judge Executive
Knochelmann has said he would not support the program until he knows the cities
are behind it as well. The Mayor added The City of Williamstown has already
passed a resolution showing their support of the program and he hopes by
Independence passing it as well, other cities will begin discussing the need
for a needle exchange program.
Jason Merrick, 1108 Amblewood Court, Independence - the Director of Addiction
Services at the Kenton County Detention Center, voiced his support for the
program. He stated he is a former heroin addict in long term recovery and
stated the program provides a level of empathy and understanding at a human
level. Mr. Merrick shared his story of addition and recovery; he found support
at a needle exchange program, completed treatment, is now a contributor to his
community and getting ready to close on his first home.
Marge Cook, 96 Carrie Way, Independence – expressed concern regarding the
needle exchange program bringing in all the needles off the streets and feels
that the police would have the protection they need from the poke proof gloves.
Charlotte Wethington, 13587 Madison Pike, Independence – voiced her support for
the program. She stated this program would give the City a chance to be
proactive instead of reactive and these addicts need and deserve treatment like
anyone else. Mrs. Wethington added the overdose cases at St. Elizabeth Hospital
went from 252 in 2011 up to 1,168 in 2015.
There being no further discussion, City Attorney Jack Gatlin read Resolution
No. 2016-R-02 which would support the implementation of a needle exchange
program to be administered by the Northern Kentucky Independent District Health
Department at the County Health Centers or St. Elizabeth Healthcare Hospitals
in accordance with KRS 218A-500.
Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve Resolution No. 2016-R-02.
Council Member Brinker so moved with a second by Council Member Deaton. Roll
was called and answered with 5 ayes and a no vote by Council Member Aseere.
Motion carried 5-1.
Resolution No. 2016-R-03 – Supporting a Kenton County Vacant Properties
Registration

Resolution No. 2016-R-04 – Land and Water Conservation Fund, 2016 Grant
Application
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Resolution No. 2016-R-04 which supports
the proposed grant application for the 2016 Land and Water Conservation Fund.
Mr. Gatlin read the Resolution and stated if the $75,000 grant is awarded to
the city, it would be used for the basketball court project behind the
Municipal Center. Chris Moriconi stated the awarded grant money would be used
to pave the parking lot and access road for the basketball courts and the city
would take care of the courts, hoops, painting and fencing. He stated the grant
application deadline is April 30th and it may be fall before we hear anything.
Council Member Franzen made a motion to approve Resolution No. 2016-R-04,
seconded by Council Member Brinker. Roll was called and answered unanimously.
Motion carried 6-0.

Executive Session  
At 7:09 p.m. a motion was made by Council Member Franzen and seconded by
Council Member Brinker to go into executive session in accordance with K.R.S.
61.810 (b) and K.R.S. 61.810 (c) to deliberate acquisition of real estate and
discuss pending litigation. Motion carried with all ayes.
At 8:02 p.m. a motion was made by Council Member Yeager and seconded by Council
Member Franzen to resume the regular meeting. Motion carried with all ayes.
Resolution No. 2016-R-05 – Regarding Health Department RFP
Mayor Reinersman presented Resolution No. 2016-R-05 to Council which is a
resolution that would authorize and approve the Mayor to negotiate financial
incentives to the Northern Kentucky Health District for the location of its
principal offices in Independence at the intersection of Turkeyfoot Road and
Industrial Road. The Mayor stated the Northern Kentucky Health District has
been looking at properties to build their new administrative offices and have
narrowed it down to Florence and Independence. He stated the incentives
included in Independence’s offer is a $100,000 discount off the purchase price
of the property as well as exterior maintenance services including grass
cutting and snow removal for up to 20 years. He stated this would be an
opportunity to stir significant economic development on the west side of the
city. He added this new office building would bring 80 employees with a $4
million plus payroll and would generate $50,000 in payroll taxes per year for
the city. The Mayor stated the City would recoup the $100,000 incentive money
back in a little over 2 years and after the property maintenance costs, the
City would still bring in $43,000 a year in payroll taxes from this site. He
added that Florence’s proposal included a higher purchase price for the land as
well as a property maintenance costs to the Health Department of $1600 a month.
The Mayor stated the Independence site at Turkeyfoot Road and Industrial Road
has been sitting empty for 12 years and an office building would help generate
interest for additional development in that area.
Council Member Franzen stated the more businesses that locate in Independence
will generate more payroll tax for the city which would result in lower real
estate tax costs for residents. Council Member Aseere stated he supports this
proposal because the City will break even in less than 5 years, Independence is
offering a lower purchase price over Florence, the payroll tax percentage is
cheaper in Independence versus Florence and Independence is also close to the
highway.
Council Member Deaton stated that while incentives can be hard to digest, he
thinks it makes sense for the Northern Kentucky Health District to keep their
office in Kenton County, which is centrally located within the district.
The Mayor stated he thinks the City has a great site and hopes the Northern
Kentucky Health District Board recognizes that when they meet to decide. He
added the incentives he proposed were needed to keep Independence in the
running as an option for the Northern Kentucky Health Department’s new site.
Council Member Franzen made a motion to approve Resolution No. 2016-R-05,
seconded by Council Member Aseere. Roll was called and answered 5 ayes and 1 no
vote by Council Member Bushong. Motion carried 5-1.
Attorney’s Report – Jack Gatlin
Mr. Gatlin stated the sewer lateral line litigation against the Sanitation
District No. 1 (SD1) has not yet been filed because cities are still joining
the lawsuit. He added, that having more cities involved, would help resolve the
issue without having to file suit. He stated there are currently 12 cities that
have passed resolutions to support a declaratory judgement that SD1 should be
responsible for all lateral line repairs within the right-a-way. Mr. Gatlin
added that progress was made when multiple city officials and SD1
representatives met to discuss this issue. He stated the interlocal agreement
is being redrafted and will take away some of the issues and SD1 appears to be
accepting responsibility for lateral line repairs.
City Administrator Report – Christian J. Moriconi
Mr. Moriconi stated he had nothing to report.
Mayor’s Report – Christopher J. Reinersman
Executive Order No. 2016-EO-03 - Mayor Reinersman presented Executive Order No.
2016-EO-03 appointing Lisa Long to the Independence Senior Board.
Council Member Franzen made a motion to approve Executive Order No. 2016-EO-03,
seconded by Council Member Deaton. Roll was called and answered unanimously.
Motion carried 6-0.
In other business, regarding the Needle Exchange Program, Mayor Reinersman
stated the city’s recommendation for the Program discussed at last month’s
Council meeting would have to be administered at one of the Northern Kentucky
Health Department clinics. He stated if the Northern Kentucky Health Department
decides on Independence for their new administrative offices, it wouldn’t mean
a Needle Exchange Program would operate at that location. He clarified that by
statute, City Council would have to pass an ordinance approving the addition of
a clinic before anything like that could happen at that location.
Council Member Brinker stated the Easter Egg Hunt will be on March 19th at noon
in Memorial Park and is for ages 9 and under. He added there will be prizes and
at least 7,000 eggs.
Council Member Franzen thanked the Public Works Department for painting lines
on Declaration Drive at the intersection of Shaw Road as she suggested at the
previous Council Meeting.
Council Member Deaton asked if Council was still interested in pursuing the
Rental License Application Registration that was discussed at the last month’s
Council Meeting. Mayor Reinersman stated it had been tabled indefinitely but
welcomed help from Council if they are interested in pursuing the program.
Council Member Deaton stated he will look into it.
Adjournment
There being no further business, a motion was made by Council Member Franzen
and seconded by Council Member Yeager to adjourn. Motion carried with all ayes
and the meeting ended at 8:22 p.m.

Opening
The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, April 4,
2016 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal Center,
5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher Reinersman
presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened with the

was called and the following Council Members registered present: Bill Aseere,
Tom Brinker, Jim Bushong, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and Donna Yeager. Also
present was City Clerk Patricia Taney, Assistant City Clerk Gina Gabbard and
City Attorney Jack Gatlin. City Administrator Chris Moriconi was absent due to
a training conference he was attending out of town.
Approval of the March 7, 2016 Regular Meeting Minutes
Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve the minutes of the regular
meeting held on March 7, 2016. Council Member Bushong so moved, with a second
by Council Member Franzen. No amendment to the minutes were noted, roll was
called and answered with all ayes. Motion carried 6-0.
Proclamation – Recognize Sophie Skinner
Mayor Reinersman presented a Proclamation to Sophie Skinner to recognize her
outstanding swimming accomplishments including four Olympic Trial qualifying
cuts and setting two State records. Sophie is also an honor roll student at
Notre Dame Academy. Council Member Franzen spoke a few words as one of Sophie’s
previous swim coaches.

Mayor Reinersman presented a Proclamation to recognize the month of April 2016
as Child Abuse Prevention Month. The Mayor thanked the City Clerk and City
staff for displaying the blue ribbons on the trees outside the Municipal Center
and encouraged citizens to do the same.
Award Bid – Holton Drive Reconstruction
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council the four bids that were received for the
Holton Drive reconstruction project. The Mayor stated this road project within
the Industrial Park is critical and he realizes it’s a lot of money to spend on
one road. He stated in 2015, Holton Drive generated over $500,000 of revenue
for the City in occupational taxes, real estate taxes and tangible taxes which
equates to about 7% of the City’s general fund revenue. The Mayor stated Len
Riegler Blacktop presented the lowest bid amount of $733,695.75 which includes
removing the concrete road and replacing with asphalt pavement. There were some
questions from Council regarding the differences between concrete and asphalt.
The Mayor stated asphalt is a better option for this project due to the amount
of traffic and is less costly to replace than concrete. He stated the road
project should start in July and be completed by the first of November.
Council Member Franzen made a motion to accept the bid from Len Riegler
Blacktop in the amount of $733,695.75 for the Holton Drive reconstruction
project, seconded by Council Member Brinker. Roll was called and answered
unanimously. Motion carried 6-0.
Memorandum of Understanding with Kenton County for Pelly Road Bridge
Reconstruction Project
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council the Memorandum of Understanding between
Kenton County and the City for combined efforts to complete the Pelly Road
Bridge reconstruction project. The Mayor stated Kenton County will provide and
assist with in-kind services for the Pelly Road Bridge reconstruction project
if the City agrees to be fully responsible for the anticipated expenditures. He
stated the estimated cost of construction is $225,175.50 which would be the
City's responsibility. He added Kenton County will be covering the cost of in-
kind assistance which is estimated at $125,000.00 and the Kenton County’s
Public Works Department will be doing most of the work. The Mayor stated the
City’s portion of the project will be funded with the $100,000 received from
the State Road Aid as well as funds in the Fowler Creek Sewer Fund. He stated
the project would include installing a giant culvert pipe which is
approximately 38 feet in diameter. The Mayor stated the goal is to have the
Pelly Road bridge re-opened before school starts back up in August. He added
this option should be completed by the August 5th deadline and would provide a
long term fix to the bridge.
Council Member Aseere made a motion to approve the Memorandum of Understanding
with Kenton County for the Pelly Road Bridge reconstruction project, seconded
by Council Member Yeager. Roll was called and answered unanimously. Motion
carried 6-0.
Declare Surplus Property – 2007 Dodge Chargers

white 2007 Dodge Charger which need to be declared surplus property. The Mayor

COUNCIL MEETING
May 2, 2016
Opening
The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, May 2,
2016 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal Center,
5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher Reinersman
presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened with the
Pledge of Allegiance and a moment of silence. Roll was called and the following
Council Members registered present: Bill Aseere, Tom Brinker, Lucas Deaton,
Carol Franzen and Donna Yeager. Jim Bushong was absent. Also present was City
Administrator Chris Moriconi, City Clerk Patricia Taney, Assistant City Clerk
Gina Gabbard and City Attorney Jack Gatlin.
Approval of the April 4, 2016 Regular Meeting Minutes
Mayor Reinersman called for a motion to approve the minutes of the regular
meeting held on April 4, 2016. Council Member Yeager so moved, with a second by
Council Member Franzen. No amendment to the minutes were noted, roll was called
and answered with all ayes. Motion carried 5-0.
Proclamation – Building Safety Month
Mayor Reinersman presented a Proclamation to recognize the month of May 2016 as
Building Safety Month.
Proposed Ordinance – Zoning Map Amendment – 45 Acres located on the NE corner
of the Intersection of Cox Road with Fowler Creek Road – 1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council a proposed ordinance to approve a zoning
map amendment to change the zone of 45 acres located at the NE corner of the
intersection of Cox Road and Fowler Creek Road from R-1C zone to R-1D. The
Mayor stated the Bridges family owns the property and are planning to develop
the land. He stated the current zone of R-1C allows homes to be built on 80
foot lots. He stated Greg Bridges is requesting a zone change to R-1D which is
a higher density zone and the change would decrease the minimum lot size from
12,500 square feet to 9,000 square feet. The Mayor stated by changing the zone
to R-1D, approximately 80 homes could be built instead of 70. He stated Mr.
Bridges is working with the City in regards to possible building conditions,
along with the approved zone change. The Mayor stated Mr. Bridges has agreed to
provide at least 80% of the homes in the development with a minimum of 25%
brick and/or stone on the front elevation. The Mayor stated he drove through
the Lakefield subdivision and calculated about 22% of existing homes have brick
on the front elevation.
The Mayor stated there are concerns regarding the streets being torn up during
construction and the idea of adding an alternate entrance has been discussed.
He stated Mr. Bridges has agreed to put in a temporary alternate entrance if he
can do so for less than $10,000.
Mr. Gatlin stated the Kenton County Planning Commission (KCPC) had the
statutory public hearing regarding this proposed zone change on April 7, 2016
and KCPC has recommended approval of the zone change with the condition that
the development density doesn’t exceed four housing units per net acre. He
stated Council’s options at this meeting are to either vote to agree/approve
with KCPC’s recommendation as is, impose additional conditions on the KCPC
recommendation, or to vote to overturn KCPC’s recommendation but approve with
conditions; each option must have at least four votes. He advised if there
isn’t a vote of at least four out of five to take action, then KCPC’s
recommendation would move forward 90 days from the date of the KCPC public
hearing (April 7, 2016) with approval for zone change with only the density
condition.
The Mayor stated twelve residents have signed in to address Council on this
proposed zone change.
Norman Davidson, 779 Jimae Avenue, Independence - voiced his concerns regarding
the plans for the new development. He urged Council could speak to Mr. Bridges
again to ask him to consider using the land as a nature center instead of
another residential development.
The Mayor stated this was discussed and Mr. Bridges stated he may donate a
portion of the land between Cox Rd and Jimae Avenue to The Kenton Conservancy.
Mike Robbins, 778 Jimae Avenue, Independence – expressed his concern regarding
the increased traffic this development would bring for families living in the
Lakefield Subdivision. He suggested the City delay action on this map amendment
and request the State permit a second entrance off Fowler Creek Road.
The Mayor stated Council has ninety days to act or KCPC’s recommendation
becomes formal approval.
Al Daly, 10330 Limerick Circle, Independence - voiced his concerns regarding
the public safety issue that would occur with this zone change. He stated homes
being so close together without a brick wrap increase exposure risks and a fire
could spread easier than if homes were farther apart. He stated the single
entrance also creates a traffic safety issue
Pam Burton, 6415 Lakearbor, Independence – voiced her concerns regarding the
additional traffic and lack of having an additional ingress/egress. She thanked
the Mayor for joining the neighborhood discussion on Facebook about this issue,
and for driving around the neighborhood counting houses, as well as trying to
help the Lakefield community in this situation. Ms. Burton stated her
disappointment that Mr. Bridges was not present to hear residents’ concerns.
She stated the construction traffic and additional vehicle traffic the new
homes will bring present safety concerns for the animals and children. Ms.
Burton stated Waterview is being torn up and there has been mud and rock debris
on the roads.
The Mayor advised the street damage is being monitored by the Public Works
Director. He stated Lakefield Subdivision is scheduled for street resurfacing
this summer. He stated the existing conditions will be addressed and will be
the builder’s responsibility to clean up the streets during and after
construction. The Mayor stated builders can be fined and/or denied permits if
existing street conditions aren’t maintained.
Wayne Erpenbeck from Erpenbeck Consulting Engineers handed out an updated plan
of the proposed development of The Woods of Lakefield as the proposed R-1D
zone. Erpenbeck Consulting Engineers have partnered with Greg Bridges of
Celestial Homes on the development plan for The Woods of Lakefield. Mr.
Erpenbeck stated by changing this zone to R-1D, the lots will be deeper and
less trees will be cut down. He stated per the plans, there will only be two
dwelling units per acre, which is below the KCPC’s recommendation of four units
per acre.
Kathleen Daley, 842 Ridgepoint Drive, Independence – voiced her support of the
zone change after hearing Council’s comments and conditions that Council added.
Dusty Poe, 875 Ridgepoint Drive, Independence – questioned if these new homes
would cause the Fowler Creek Sewer system to be re-assessed.
The Mayor stated the last payment of the Fowler Creek Sewer loan has been paid
and there will be no additional assessments payments by the residents.
Donald Barnett, 788 Jimae Avenue, Independence – voiced his concern regarding
the street damage during construction. He stated there have been twenty-five
trucks with fill dirt, going up and down Jimae daily for this new development.
Mr. Barnett presented pictures to Council showing current damage to Jimae.
Mr. Moriconi stated the Public Works Director Dan Koch and Mr. Bridges will be
reviewing and discussing the damage caused by the construction and it will be
repaired.
Gregory Bridges, Owner of Celestial Homes addressed questions by Council. He
stated the homes will range in size from 1100 to 1800 square feet and sale
prices will range from $130,000 to $173,000. Mr. Bridges stated the zone change
will allow for larger homes on a smaller lot for the same price of smaller
homes on a larger lot. He stated the homes will be on-site, stick build homes
and will include both market homes as well as contracts to build on vacant
lots. He stated the R-1D zone will allow less homes built per acre than KCPC’s
recommendations. Mr. Bridges stated an alternate entrance idea has been
explored but the State did not want another street coming through on Cox Road
citing inadequate site distance to add an entrance on Fowler Creek Road. He
stated there are plans to provide a temporary access for construction vehicles
at the bottom of Cox Road.
Andy Videkovich, Planning Manager for Planning and Development Services
addressed Council by stating the development plan that was submitted shows
approximately two dwelling units per acre and the KCPC’s recommendation was
four or less units per acre. He stated a development plan is not required nor
can be bound with the current zone which is R1-C. Mr. Videkovich stated both
Lakefield Drive and Lakearbor Drive were built to the sub-collector standard
which means they can handle traffic for up to 500 lots without having a second
entrance. He stated there are currently about 400 dwelling units, so it can
handle the additional 70 to 80 lots Mr. Bridges is planning to build.
Mr. Gatlin stated that in order for Council to move forward with accepting
KCPC’s recommendation and additional conditions, a motion would need to be made
and have at least 4 favorable votes to result in a first reading. He stated
Council’s motion would be to accept KCPC’s recommendation to approve the zone
change including the condition of four units or less per net acre. Mr. Gatlin
stated two additional conditions expressed by Council were 1) to have at least
80% of home fronts contain a minimum of 25% brick and/or stone during any point
during construction and 2) to construct an alternate entrance from either
Fowler Creek Road or Cox Road during the initial development phase as
allowable, which would facilitate construction traffic for any vehicles heavier
than a concrete truck; if the cost of the alternate entrance exceeds $10,000,
the City can waive the requirement or opt to cover the cost difference.
Mayor Reinersman asked Council for a motion to accept KCPC’s recommendation to
approve the zone change including the condition of 4 units or less per net acre
as well as the two additional conditions stated by Mr. Gatlin. Council Member
Franzen so moved, seconded by Council Member Brinker. Roll was called and
answered unanimously. Motion carried 5-0.
Mayor Reinersman presented the proposed ordinance to Council, which accepts
KCPC’s recommendation to amend the zoning map for the 45 acres located at the
northeast intersection of Cox Road and Fowler Creek Road in Independence from
R-1C zone to R-1D zone with three conditions pertaining to density, brick/stone
on house fronts and a temporary alternate construction entrance. Mr. Gatlin
gave the ordinance a first reading which included the three conditions of
approval by the Council.
Award Bid – Pelly Road Bridge
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council the bid received for the culvert pipe for
the Pelly Road Bridge replacement. He stated the sole bidder was Contech
Engineered Solutions with a bid of $50,275 which was $25,425 less than the
engineers estimate. The Mayor stated the environmental report has been sub-

Resolution No. 2016-R-07 - Rumpke Contract Renewal for Curbside Trash and
Recycling Pickup
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Resolution No. 2016-R-07 which is a
resolution authorizing and approving the Mayor to execute an extension of the
previously bid fees for trash and recycling services for residential units in
the City. The Mayor thanked Mr. Moriconi, Ms. Taney and Attorney Brandon Volker
for their hard work on this contract which resulted in additional services from
Rumpke while keeping a good price.
Mr. Moriconi stated the two year extension is being utilized and addendums have

after 8:30 a.m. on the main roads of Madison Pike, Turkeyfoot Road and
Independence Station Road, and continued service on vacant and delinquent
properties. He stated Rumpke will continue to pick up trash and collect
payments from property owners. He stated each year around June 30th, Rumpke

billing issue.
Mayor Reinersman asked Council for a motion to approve Resolution No. 2016-R-07

Proposed Ordinance – Adopting 2016-2017 Budget – 1st Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council the proposed ordinance which adopts the
annual budget for the Fiscal Year beginning July 1, 2016 and ending June 30,
2017. In his budget address Mayor Reinersman stated the primary focus is
funding infrastructure while continuing to maintain other services. He stated
two major infrastructure projects in this budget include the replacement of
Holton Drive and the Pelly Road Bridge. Mayor Reinersman stated the recently
updated street inventory report concluded the City needs to invest over a
million dollars per year to maintain City streets. He stated street repairs
will be a priority and one million dollars will be invested to maintain and
replace roads within the City. He stated this budget allows the City to move
forward while minimizing the impact on the residents and keeping fund reserves
at a safe level. Mr. Gatlin gave the proposed ordinance a first reading.

Mr. Gatlin stated his one year anniversary of being the City Attorney is coming

work with.
City Administrator Report – Chris Moriconi
Mr. Moriconi announced the Kelly Miller Circus is coming to town on May 13th
and 14th. He stated the show times are Friday, May 13th at 4:30 p.m. and 7:30
p.m. and Saturday, May 14th at 2:00 p.m. and 5:00 p.m.
He complimented Council Member Yeager and Parks and Recreations Director Nita
Brake for their fundraising efforts for the Fourth of July Celebration and
advised that $26,000 has been raised so far.
Mayor’s Report – Chris Reinersman
Mayor Reinersman advised that after a long process, the nomination application
has been submitted to the National Heritage Council for the City’s downtown
area to be designated as a Historical District. He stated on May 3rd at 6:30
p.m., the Kentucky Heritage Council will be hosting a public information
session in the Council Chambers to discuss what it means to be a Historical
District. He extended an invitation to interested residents to attend. He
stated the benefits of having a Historical District are: it draws attention for
future businesses, creates incentives for rehab, it allows for commercial
properties and federal and state tax credits. The Mayor stated the Kentucky
Preservation Review Board will decide on May 20, 2016 in Frankfort whether or
not to designate downtown Independence as a Historical District.
Mayor Reinersman stated his appreciation to generous local businesses that
collectively donated 100 tickets for the upcoming Kelly Miller Circus
performances. He stated the donated tickets have been distributed to schools
and day care centers within the City. The Mayor also expressed his thanks to
the Deters Company for permitting the City to use the vacant lot in the
Independence Towne Center for the circus set up again this year.

Police Academy that graduated on April 26, 2016. He stated the next class will
be in the spring of 2017 and encouraged interested citizens to submit their
applications. The Mayor thanked Chief Lucas, Sergeant Boyle, Officer Bridges,
Mrs. Weger and Mrs. Runge as well as the entire police department for their
hard work with this program.
Mr. Moriconi and Mayor Reinersman recognized Finance Director Terri Hudson for
her hard work on the budgets.
Adjournment

and seconded by Council Member Yeager to adjourn. Motion carried with all ayes
and the meeting ended at 8:53 p.m.

COUNCIL MEETING
June 6, 2016
Opening
The City Council of the City of Independence, Kentucky met on Monday, June 6,
2016 at 7:00 p.m. in the Council Chambers of the Independence Municipal Center,
5409 Madison Pike, Independence, Kentucky with Mayor Christopher Reinersman
presiding. Mayor Reinersman called the meeting to order and opened with the
Pledge of Allegiance and Council Member Bushong led the invocation. Roll was
called and the following Council Members registered present: Bill Aseere, Tom
Brinker, Jim Bushong, Lucas Deaton, Carol Franzen and Donna Yeager. Also
present was City Administrator Chris Moriconi, City Clerk Patricia Taney,
Assistant City Clerk Gina Gabbard and City Attorney Jack Gatlin.
Kenton County Judge Executive Kris Knochelmann
Judge Executive Kris Knochelmann addressed Council with updates regarding the
Digital Radio Project occurring within Kenton County. He stated in February of
2015, Trott’s Public Safety Radio System Analysis and Recommendations Report
evaluated the Kenton County dispatch systems, which is several decades old.
Judge Knochelmann stated himself and the judges in Campbell, Boone and Grant
counties have agreed to spend approximately five million dollars to update the
technology for first responders within the community.
Kenton County Administrator Joe Schreiber addressed Council and stated the
analysis performed on the current dispatch systems identified that 7 out of the
9 major infrastructure components would be unsupported or obsolete by 2018. He
stated the research showed the current Analog system could be updated for
approximately five million dollars. Mr. Schreiber stated the second option is
to upgrade to the digital 800Mhz system for an additional six hundred and
thirty seven thousand dollars. He stated the benefits of the digital system are
worth the additional cost. He stated the formulation and building of the new
infrastructure will begin in August of 2016, radio bids will be awarded around
April 2017 and the projected go-live date for the new digital system is
estimated for mid 2018.
Police Business – New Officers and Explorers Competition Recognition
Mayor Reinersman swore in new Police Recruits Ben Bridges and Michael Haught.
Chief Lucas recognized the Explorers for their participation in the Southwest
Ohio Regional Explorers Competition in May 2016. He stated the Independence
Explorers competed against 19 other teams and placed 5th overall. He added
Sergeant Tyler Runge placed first in the driving obstacle course individual
competition. Chief Lucas expressed his thanks to each of the Explorers and to
the Officers that have trained them. Mayor Reinersman also thanked the
Explorers for their time and effort.
Mayor Reinersman presented Chief Lucas with a plaque in celebration of his 25
years of service with the Independence Police Department. Chief Lucas thanked
the Mayor and said a few words.
Approval of the May 2, 2016 Regular Meeting Minutes
Mayor Reinersman stated a couple corrections to the minutes for the regular
meeting held on May 2, 2016; changes were noted. The Mayor called for a motion
to approve the minutes as amended for the regular meeting held on May 2, 2016.
Council Member Brinker so moved, with a second by Council Member Yeager. Roll
was called and answered with 5 ayes and 1 abstention from Council Member
Bushong. Motion carried.
Ordinance No. 2016-O-02 – Zoning Map Amendment – 45 Acres located on the NE
corner of the Intersection of Cox Road with Fowler Creek Road – 2nd Reading
Mayor Reinersman presented to Council Ordinance No. 2016-O-02 which accepts
KCPC’s recommendation to amend the zoning map for the 45 acres located at the
northeast intersection of Cox Road and Fowler Creek Road in Independence from
R-1C zone to R-1D zone with three conditions pertaining to density, brick/stone
on house fronts and a temporary alternate construction entrance. Mr. Gatlin
gave the ordinance a second reading which included KCPC’s recommendation of
changing the zone to R-1C with the condition of four units or less per net
acre. Mr. Gatlin stated two additional conditions expressed by Council 1) to
have at least 80% of home fronts contain a minimum of 25% brick and/or stone
during any point during construction and 2) to construct an alternate entrance
from Fowler Creek Road during the initial development phase as allowable, which
would facilitate construction traffic for vehicles heavier than a concrete
truck; if the cost of the alternate entrance exceeds $10,000, the City can
waive the requirement or opt to cover the cost difference.
Council Member Franzen made a motion to approve Ordinance No. 2016-O-02,
seconded by Council Member Aseere. Roll was called and answered unanimously.
Motion carried 6-0.
